01_Metal_properties_determine_uses.json.title: Metal properties determine uses
01_Metal_properties_determine_uses.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Compare the general physical properties of metals and non-metals, and describe how a given metal reacts with cold water, steam and dilute acid.
Explain a stated use of aluminium or copper by matching the use to the specific physical property that makes the metal suitable, including cases where more than one property is needed together.

prerequisites.statement: Metallic bonding is a lattice of positive metal ions in a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move through the whole structure.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Electrical and thermal conductivity, and the ability of layers of atoms to slide over each other, both follow directly from this structure, not from any property of a single isolated atom.

prerequisites.statement: A metal reacting with an acid produces a salt and hydrogen gas, and a more vigorous reaction gives faster bubbling.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Reading reactivity differences from the speed of bubbling with an acid is a skill this lesson reuses directly for water and steam.

diagnostic_items.question: A metal conducts electricity well. Does this guarantee it is also light in weight for its size? Answer in one sentence.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: No: electrical conductivity comes from the delocalised electrons in the metallic lattice, while density depends on how heavy and how closely packed the atoms are, which is an independent property.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Yes, metals that conduct well are always light, like aluminium.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has generalised from one familiar example (aluminium) into a rule linking two unrelated properties.

common_wrong_answers.answer: No, because metals don't conduct electricity well at all.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is confusing metals with non-metals, or has not yet accepted conductivity as a defining metallic property.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks whether the learner treats 'metal' as a single bundle of properties that all vary together, instead of as several independent properties that happen to co-occur in a given metal by coincidence of its structure.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Put copper (dense, excellent conductor) next to aluminium (light, good conductor) side by side and ask the learner to name one property they share and one they do not.

diagnostic_items.question: A strip of magnesium and a strip of zinc are dropped into separate test tubes of dilute hydrochloric acid. Both strips bubble, but the magnesium bubbles much faster. Name the gas being given off, and state what the difference in bubbling rate tells you about the two metals.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: The gas is hydrogen. Magnesium bubbles faster, so magnesium reacts more vigorously with the acid than zinc does, which means magnesium is the more reactive of the two metals. Each reaction also produces a salt: magnesium chloride in one tube and zinc chloride in the other.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The gas is carbon dioxide, and the faster bubbling shows the magnesium is purer.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has recalled the carbonate-plus-acid test instead of the metal-plus-acid reaction, and is explaining the rate difference by sample quality rather than by reactivity.

common_wrong_answers.answer: The gas is hydrogen, but the bubbling rate only shows that the magnesium strip was bigger.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner names the product correctly but does not yet read rate of bubbling as evidence about the metal itself, which is exactly the inference this lesson reuses for water and steam.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks the two halves of the prerequisite together: that a metal with a dilute acid gives a salt and hydrogen, and that faster bubbling under the same conditions means a more vigorous, more reactive metal. Both are reused immediately when the same comparison is made with cold water and steam.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Set the two reactions side by side with equal-sized strips in the same acid, and ask the learner to time how long each takes to stop bubbling before naming which metal is more reactive.

theory_blocks.title: A property has to match a job
theory_blocks.body:
An engineer choosing a material for an overhead power cable, a cooking pan, or a drinks can never asks 'is this a good metal?' in general.

They ask a narrower question: does this specific sample have [[blue:the specific measured property]] the job needs, in a high enough amount, at an acceptable cost?

A cooking pan base needs high thermal conductivity, so heat spreads quickly and evenly rather than scorching one spot. An aircraft panel needs low density, so the whole aircraft is not too heavy to fly efficiently.

A drinks can needs corrosion resistance, so the metal does not react with the drink or with damp air during storage.

The same element, aluminium, happens to satisfy all three jobs reasonably well, which is exactly why it appears in cookware, aircraft and drinks cans for three different reasons.

theory_blocks.title: Metal and non-metal properties compared
theory_blocks.body:
Metals, as a class, tend to share a set of physical properties that follow from metallic bonding: a lattice of positive ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons that are free to move.

- **Good electrical conductors**, because the delocalised electrons can drift through the whole structure when a voltage is applied.
- **Good thermal conductors**, because the same mobile electrons transfer kinetic energy through the lattice quickly.
- **Malleable and ductile**: the layers of metal ions can slide over one another without breaking the metallic bond, so a metal can be hammered into sheets or drawn into wires without shattering.
- **High melting and boiling points** (with a few exceptions) and typically high density, because the lattice is held together by strong electrostatic attraction between the ions and the delocalised electrons.

Non-metals, by contrast, are typically poor conductors of electricity and heat (graphite is the well-known exception, because it also has delocalised electrons between its layers), are brittle rather than malleable when solid, and often have lower melting points.

These are **general tendencies, not exception-free rules**: stating 'metals are always...' about any property risks being wrong for a specific element, so a claim should always be checked against the specific metal in question.

assets.caption: Density of three metals in g/cm$^3$ (aluminium 2.7, iron 7.9, copper 9.0): aluminium is roughly a third as dense as copper.
assets.purpose: Gives the real comparative density data behind the claim that aluminium is a 'light' metal, rather than leaving it as an unsupported adjective.

assets.caption: Approximate relative electrical conductivity, copper taken as 100: copper conducts best, aluminium reaches about 61% of copper's conductivity, and iron only about 17%.
assets.purpose: Shows that copper's conductivity advantage over aluminium is real but not enormous, which is why aluminium's much lower density can still win the overall trade-off for a long cable.

theory_blocks.title: A use is a trade-off, not a single property
theory_blocks.body:
Overhead power cables are the clearest example of a trade-off. Copper conducts electricity better than aluminium (about 100 against about 61, on the scale above), so a copper cable of the same thickness carries current with less energy wasted as heat.

But a cable strung between pylons has to support its own weight over tens of metres without sagging too far or snapping, and aluminium's much lower density (about 2.7 against about 9.0 g/cm$^3$) means an aluminium cable thick enough to match copper's conductivity is still lighter than a thinner copper cable chosen for the same job.

For this specific use, low density is weighted more heavily than the conductivity gap, so aluminium wins; for a short wire inside a plug, where weight is irrelevant and conductivity in a small space matters more, copper wins instead.

Copper's resistance to corrosion in damp air, together with its conductivity, is also why it is used for the electrical wiring inside buildings, where the wire is protected from the much higher stresses an overhead cable faces.

theory_blocks.title: Reaction with water, steam and acid is also a property
theory_blocks.body:
Besides physical properties such as conductivity and density, a metal's **chemical** reactivity is also a property that can be observed and compared,

and it follows the same pattern: some metals react readily, some only under harsher conditions, and some barely react at all.

The general pattern, from the most to the least reactive of the metals considered here: the most reactive metals (such as potassium, sodium and calcium) react visibly with cold water, releasing hydrogen gas and forming the metal hydroxide.

Less reactive metals (such as magnesium, zinc and iron) show no clear reaction with cold water but do react with steam, forming the metal oxide and hydrogen gas.

The least reactive metals (such as copper, silver and gold) show no reaction with water in any form.

A separate but related pattern holds for dilute acid: a metal that reacts with cold water also reacts vigorously with dilute acid, and the less reactive metals that only react with steam still react with dilute acid, producing a salt and hydrogen gas, while the least reactive metals do not react with dilute acid either.

This full ordering is developed and justified from evidence in the next lesson; here, it is enough to treat 'how readily does this metal react' as one more measurable property, alongside density and conductivity.

keywords.definition: Able to be hammered or pressed into a different shape without shattering.
Able to be drawn out into a wire without breaking.
Electrons in a metallic lattice that are not attached to one particular atom and are free to move through the structure, giving metals their conductivity.
Mass per unit volume of a material, usually given in g/cm$^3$.
How well a metal resists reacting with substances such as oxygen, water or acids in its environment.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing a saucepan base.** A manufacturer must choose a metal for the base of a saucepan. State the one physical property that matters most for this use, and name a metal that provides it well.
solution: The base of a saucepan must transfer heat from the hob to the food quickly and evenly, so the property that matters most is thermal conductivity.

Copper is an excellent thermal conductor (its electrical conductivity, from the same delocalised electrons, is the highest of common metals), so copper, or a copper-bottomed pan, is a standard choice.
worked_examples.interpretation: Naming the single dominant property first, before naming a metal, avoids the common habit of listing 'copper is good' without stating why.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two cables.** An aluminium cable and a copper cable are designed to carry the same current over the same span between two pylons. Using the approximate relative conductivity (copper 100, aluminium 61) and density (copper 9.0 g/cm$^3$, aluminium 2.7 g/cm$^3$) values given earlier, explain why the aluminium cable, even though it must be made thicker to match copper's current-carrying capacity, is still the lighter overall choice.
solution: To carry the same current with a higher resistance per unit cross-section, the aluminium cable must have a larger cross-sectional area than the copper cable; roughly, it needs about $100/61 \approx 1.6$ times the cross-sectional area of the copper cable to compensate for its lower conductivity.

Mass per unit length is density multiplied by cross-sectional area, so the aluminium cable's mass per metre is approximately $2.7 \times 1.6 \approx 4.3$ 'units', compared with copper's $9.0 \times 1 = 9.0$ 'units' for the thinner cable.

Even after thickening the aluminium cable enough to match copper's conductivity, its much lower density means the finished aluminium cable is still noticeably lighter per metre than the copper cable, which is why aluminium, not copper, is used for long overhead spans.
worked_examples.interpretation:
The arithmetic (1.6 times the area, then 4.3 against 9.0 'mass units') is deliberately approximate and unit-free, since the point is the comparison, not a precise engineering value;

it shows numerically why the trade-off favours aluminium rather than asserting it.

worked_examples.statement: **A puzzling observation.** A technician drops a strip of magnesium ribbon into a beaker of cold water and sees no bubbles at all, even after several minutes. She concludes that magnesium does not react with water under any conditions. Evaluate this conclusion.
solution: The technician's observation (no visible bubbling in cold water over a few minutes) is correct, but her conclusion generalises beyond what that single observation supports.

Magnesium does react with cold water, but extremely slowly, producing bubbles too small and too infrequent to notice over a short time; a much longer observation, or a more sensitive test, would detect a slow reaction.

Magnesium reacts far more readily with steam, forming magnesium oxide and hydrogen, and with dilute acid. The correct conclusion is that magnesium is not highly reactive with cold water specifically, not that it is unreactive with water in every form.
worked_examples.interpretation:
This targets the jump from 'no reaction observed in this short test' to 'no reaction is possible';

it is the mirror image of the over-generalisation that all metals react violently with cold water, since both errors draw a general rule from one limited observation.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Treating a short, informal observation window as proof that a reaction cannot happen at all, rather than as evidence only about its rate under those conditions.

guided_exercises.statement: A company needs a metal for the casing of a mobile phone. The casing must be light enough that the phone is comfortable to hold, strong enough to survive being dropped, and must not corrode from the sweat and moisture it meets daily. Suggest a suitable metal and justify your choice using two separate properties.
hints: List the three requirements separately before choosing a metal: light, strong, corrosion-resistant.
Think about which common metal is specifically known for a naturally corrosion-resistant surface as well as low density.
A good answer names the metal once and then matches each requirement to a named property in turn, rather than giving one vague justification.
guided_exercises.answer: Aluminium (often as an aluminium alloy, for extra strength) is a suitable choice: its low density keeps the casing light, and it naturally forms a thin, tough oxide layer on its surface that resists further corrosion from moisture, protecting the metal underneath without the casing needing a separate coating.
common_errors: Choosing a metal correctly but justifying it with only one property (for example, 'aluminium is light') when the question specifically asks for two.

guided_exercises.statement: A student is given three unlabelled metal strips and told only that one is copper, one is aluminium and one is magnesium. Describe one physical test and one chemical test that, together, would let the student identify all three without using any reference book of densities.
hints: A physical test could compare how heavy each strip feels for its size, even without exact numbers, since the three metals have quite different densities.
A chemical test could use dilute acid or cold water and compare how vigorously, if at all, each strip reacts.
Combine the two tests: the physical test should separate the densest metal from the other two, and the chemical test should separate the remaining two from each other.
guided_exercises.answer: Physical test: weigh equal-sized strips (or compare their mass for a similar volume); copper is noticeably denser (about 9.0 g/cm$^3$) than aluminium (about 2.7 g/cm$^3$) or magnesium (about 1.7 g/cm$^3$), so copper is identified first by being clearly the heaviest for its size. Chemical test: place the remaining two strips in cold water (or dilute acid, more safely and more clearly for both). Magnesium reacts, very slowly with cold water or much more readily with dilute acid, releasing small bubbles of hydrogen, while aluminium shows negligible reaction with cold water and reacts only slowly with dilute acid because of its protective oxide layer; the strip that reacts more noticeably is magnesium, and the one that barely reacts is aluminium.
common_errors: Trying to use the chemical test to separate copper from the others instead of magnesium from aluminium, when copper has already been identified by density; the acid test should only need to distinguish the two remaining metals.

exercises.statement: State two physical properties shared by most metals, and for each one, name the feature of metallic bonding or structure that is responsible.
exercises.answer: Good electrical conductivity: caused by the delocalised electrons in the metallic lattice, which are free to move and carry charge through the structure. Malleability: caused by the layers of positive metal ions being able to slide over one another without breaking the overall metallic bond, since the attraction between ions and the surrounding sea of electrons does not depend on exact position.

exercises.statement: Predict, with a reason, whether you would expect to see visible bubbling within a few minutes when a strip of zinc is placed in: (a) cold water, (b) dilute hydrochloric acid.
exercises.answer: (a) No clear bubbling is expected: zinc is a moderately reactive metal that does not react visibly with cold water, only reacting with steam. (b) Bubbling is expected: zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce zinc chloride and hydrogen gas, and this reaction is clearly visible at room temperature even though zinc is less reactive than, for example, magnesium.

exercises.statement: Food cans are made from steel (mostly iron) with a very thin coating of tin on the inside surface. Suggest why tin, rather than iron, is chosen for the surface that actually touches the food, even though the can's strength comes from the steel underneath.
exercises.answer: Tin is less reactive than iron and does not react with the food or with the moisture inside the can, so it protects the iron from corrosion and keeps the food from reacting with, or being contaminated by, the metal; the steel underneath supplies the strength and rigidity the can needs, a job tin alone (being soft) could not do.
common_errors: Assuming tin must be stronger than iron because it is used on the 'important' food-facing surface, rather than recognising that corrosion resistance, not strength, is the property being used here.

exercises.statement: A new lightweight bicycle frame is advertised as being made from 'a titanium alloy, chosen for its excellent strength-to-weight ratio and corrosion resistance.' Without looking up titanium specifically, explain what a 'strength-to-weight ratio' tells a designer that density or strength alone would not, and why both properties matter for a bicycle frame in particular.
exercises.answer: A strength-to-weight ratio combines two separate properties into one: how much load a material can bear (strength) relative to how heavy a given amount of it is (density). A very strong but very dense metal could still make a frame too heavy to be practical, while a very light but weak metal could make a frame that bends or breaks; neither strength nor density alone tells a designer whether the material can bear a cyclist's weight and the stresses of riding without being needlessly heavy to carry or pedal. Corrosion resistance matters separately because a bicycle frame is exposed to rain, sweat and road grit over years of use, so a metal that corroded readily would weaken and eventually fail even if its strength-to-weight ratio was excellent when new.

exam_questions.statement: Aluminium and copper are both used to make electrical wiring, but for different purposes: copper is used inside buildings and aluminium is used for long overhead cables between pylons. Explain, using two different properties, why each metal is suited to its own use.
exam_questions.answer: Copper has the higher electrical conductivity of the two metals, so for the shorter, protected wiring inside a building, where the wire's own weight is not a significant engineering problem, copper's better conductivity (less energy wasted as heat for a given current) makes it the preferred choice. Aluminium has a much lower density than copper, so for a long overhead cable, which must support its own weight across a wide span between pylons without sagging excessively or snapping, aluminium's lower mass per metre is the more important property, even though a thicker aluminium cable is needed to match copper's current-carrying capacity.
mark_scheme: States that copper has higher electrical conductivity than aluminium.
Links copper's conductivity to its use in short, internal building wiring.
States that aluminium has lower density than copper.
Links aluminium's lower density to its use in long overhead cables, where supporting its own weight matters.

exam_questions.statement: A technician tests three metal samples, X, Y and Z, by placing each in cold water and separately in dilute hydrochloric acid, with these results: X bubbles vigorously in cold water; Y shows no reaction in cold water but bubbles steadily in dilute acid; Z shows no reaction in either cold water or dilute acid. Put X, Y and Z in order of reactivity, from most to least reactive, and justify the order using the observations given.
exam_questions.answer: The order, from most to least reactive, is X, then Y, then Z. X is the most reactive because it reacts even with cold water, a reaction only the most reactive metals show. Y is less reactive than X because it does not react with cold water, but it is still reactive enough to react with dilute acid, producing hydrogen gas. Z is the least reactive of the three because it shows no reaction with either cold water or dilute acid, placing it among the least reactive metals considered in this course.
mark_scheme: States the order X, Y, Z from most to least reactive.
Justifies X as most reactive because it reacts with cold water.
Justifies Y as intermediate: no reaction with cold water, but reacts with dilute acid.
Justifies Z as least reactive: no reaction with either cold water or dilute acid.
States that the bubbles produced (by X in water and Y in acid) are hydrogen gas.

challenge_questions.statement:
**Choosing the metal for an overhead cable.** A manufacturer must pick one metal for a long overhead power cable. The table gives approximate values for three candidates.

| Metal | Density / g per cm³ | Relative electrical conductivity (copper = 100) | Approximate cost of 1 kg / dollars |
|---|---|---|---|
| aluminium | 2.7 | 61 | 2.50 |
| copper | 9.0 | 100 | 9.00 |
| iron | 7.9 | 17 | 0.60 |

Every cable has to carry the same current with the same energy wasted as heat, so a metal with a lower conductivity must be made into a correspondingly thicker cable: the cross-sectional area needed is in inverse proportion to the conductivity. Take the copper cable to have a cross-sectional area of 1.0 cm².

(a) Calculate the cross-sectional area needed for an aluminium cable and for an iron cable.
(b) Calculate the mass of 1 metre of each of the three cables, in kg. (One metre of cable of cross-sectional area A cm² has a volume of 100A cm³, and 1000 g = 1 kg.)
(c) Calculate the cost of the metal in 1 metre of each cable.
(d) Iron is by far the cheapest of the three per kilogram. Using your answers, explain why iron is still not the best choice, and state which metal you would recommend for this use and why.
hints: For (a), the area must rise by exactly the factor the conductivity falls by: area $= 1.0 \times 100 \div \text{conductivity}$.
For (b), find the volume of one metre first (100 × area, in cm³), multiply by the density to get a mass in grams, then divide by 1000 to get kilograms.
For (d), compare the three costs per metre, not the costs per kilogram: a metal that is cheap per kilogram stops being cheap if the cable needs five or six times as much of it.
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Aluminium: $1.0 \times \dfrac{100}{61} = 1.64\text{ cm}^2$. Iron: $1.0 \times \dfrac{100}{17} = 5.88\text{ cm}^2$.

(b) Copper: volume $= 100 \times 1.0 = 100\text{ cm}^3$, mass $= 100 \times 9.0 = 900$ g $= 0.90$ kg. Aluminium: volume $= 100 \times 1.64 = 164\text{ cm}^3$, mass $= 164 \times 2.7 = 443$ g $= 0.44$ kg. Iron: volume $= 100 \times 5.88 = 588\text{ cm}^3$, mass $= 588 \times 7.9 = 4647$ g $= 4.65$ kg.

(c) Copper: $0.90 \times 9.00 = 8.1$ dollars per metre. Aluminium: $0.44 \times 2.50 = 1.1$ dollars per metre. Iron: $4.65 \times 0.60 = 2.8$ dollars per metre.

(d) Iron costs least per kilogram, but its conductivity is only 17 against copper's 100, so an iron cable needs nearly six times the cross-sectional area of the copper one; combined with iron's high density that gives about 4.65 kg of metal per metre, more than ten times the aluminium cable's 0.44 kg, and about 2.8 dollars per metre against aluminium's 1.1. The low price per kilogram is cancelled out by how much iron the cable needs. Aluminium is the recommendation: it gives both the smallest mass per metre (0.44 kg) and the lowest cost per metre (about 1.1 dollars), and for an overhead cable that must support its own weight between pylons the mass per metre is the property that matters most.
common_errors: Recommending iron because it has the lowest cost per kilogram, without working out how much more iron a cable of the same current-carrying capacity actually needs.
Comparing the three densities directly, as if all three cables would be made the same thickness.

mcq.stem: Which property is the main reason aluminium, rather than copper, is used for long overhead power cables?

options.text: Aluminium's higher electrical conductivity
options.why_wrong: aluminium's electrical conductivity is lower than copper's, not higher; this is the opposite of the true comparison.

options.text: Aluminium's lower cost alone, regardless of weight
options.why_wrong: cost is a real factor in some choices, but for this specific use the decisive engineering reason is the cable's own weight over a long span, not price alone.

options.text: Aluminium's lower density
Aluminium conducts heat better than it conducts electricity
options.why_wrong: this compares two properties of aluminium to each other rather than comparing aluminium with copper, and is not the reason given for this use.

mcq.explanation: Aluminium's much lower density means a cable of adequate strength and conductivity still weighs less per metre than a copper cable, which matters over the long, unsupported span between pylons.

mcq.stem: A strip of metal shows no reaction when placed in cold water, but bubbles steadily when placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. What can be concluded about this metal?

options.text: It is completely unreactive and the bubbling must be a measurement error.
options.why_wrong: steady, reproducible bubbling in acid is a genuine reaction, not an error; this option ignores the evidence given.

options.text: It is one of the most reactive metals, such as potassium or sodium.
options.why_wrong: the most reactive metals react visibly with cold water itself; a metal that shows no reaction with cold water cannot be one of these.

options.text: It cannot be a metal at all, since all metals react with cold water.
options.why_wrong: this assumes every metal reacts with cold water, which is the misconception that only the most reactive metals actually do so.

options.text: It reacts with dilute acid but is not among the small group of metals reactive enough to react visibly with cold water.

mcq.explanation: Reacting with dilute acid but not with cold water is exactly the pattern shown by moderately reactive metals such as magnesium, zinc or iron, which sit below the most reactive metals but above the least reactive ones.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly compares the general properties of metals and non-metals?

options.text: Metals tend to be malleable and good conductors, but these are general tendencies rather than exception-free rules.
Metals are always better electrical conductors than non-metals, without exception.
options.why_wrong: graphite, a non-metal, is also a good electrical conductor because it has delocalised electrons between its layers, so 'without exception' is too strong a claim.

options.text: Non-metals are always brittle and metals are always malleable in every physical state.
options.why_wrong: mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature, so 'malleable in every physical state' cannot be correct as an absolute statement about all metals.

options.text: Density is higher for every metal than for every non-metal.
options.why_wrong: lithium, sodium and potassium are all metals with densities lower than several common non-metal solids, so this absolute comparison is false.

mcq.explanation: The properties associated with metals (conductivity, malleability, high density, high melting point) are genuine tendencies that follow from metallic bonding, but graphite, mercury and the low-density alkali metals are well-known exceptions that make 'always' claims incorrect.

mcq.stem: A drinks can is made from aluminium. Which pair of properties best explains this choice?

options.text: High density and high electrical conductivity
options.why_wrong: high density would be an unwanted property for a drinks can, which benefits from being light; this pairing does not match the actual requirement.

options.text: Low density and good resistance to corrosion from the drink and from damp air
High melting point and strong magnetism
options.why_wrong: a drinks can is never heated anywhere near a metal's melting point, and magnetism plays no role in its function; neither property is relevant here.

options.text: Low cost and bright colour only
options.why_wrong: cost matters to the manufacturer but is not a property of the metal itself, and colour does not explain why a can should be light and resist corrosion; neither explains the choice.

mcq.explanation: A can needs to be light to transport cheaply and must not corrode from contact with the drink or with moisture in the air; aluminium's low density and naturally protective oxide layer satisfy both requirements.

flashcards.front: Name three physical properties typical of metals.
flashcards.back: Good electrical conductivity, good thermal conductivity, and malleability (can be hammered into shape without shattering).

flashcards.front: What products form when a metal reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
flashcards.back: A metal chloride salt and hydrogen gas, for example $\mathrm{Mg} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$.

flashcards.front: Why is aluminium chosen for overhead power cables but copper is chosen for wiring inside a building?
flashcards.back: Aluminium's much lower density matters most over a long, self-supporting overhead span; copper's higher conductivity matters most for shorter, supported indoor wiring.

flashcards.front: Does every metal bubble vigorously when placed in cold water?
flashcards.back: No. Only the most reactive metals (such as potassium, sodium and calcium) react visibly with cold water; most other metals do not.

flashcards.front: A food can's inside surface is coated with tin rather than left as bare steel. What property of tin is being used?
flashcards.back: Tin's low reactivity (corrosion resistance), which protects the iron in the steel from reacting with the food or moisture inside the can.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: All metals react violently with cold water.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The dramatic, widely shown reactions of sodium or potassium with water are the first metal-water reactions many learners see, so the behaviour gets generalised to 'metal' as a category.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts bubbling or fizzing when iron or copper is placed in cold water.
misconceptions.correct_model: Reaction with cold water is a property of the most reactive metals only (such as potassium, sodium and calcium); magnesium reacts only very slowly, and metals such as zinc, iron, copper, silver and gold show no visible reaction with cold water at all.
misconceptions.remediation: Place a strip of magnesium and a strip of sodium in separate beakers of cold water and compare what is actually observed over the same short time, rather than assuming both behave the same way.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Aluminium is chosen for overhead power cables only because it is cheap.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Cost is a factor learners hear about in everyday contexts, so it is assumed to be the whole explanation whenever a cheaper material is chosen over a 'better' one like copper.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner justifies the choice of aluminium using price alone, without mentioning mass or the cable's own weight.
misconceptions.correct_model: Aluminium is chosen for long overhead cables mainly because of its low density: a cable needs to support its own weight between pylons without sagging or snapping, and aluminium's lower mass per metre matters more here than its lower conductivity compared with copper.
misconceptions.remediation: Give the mass per metre of an aluminium cable and a copper cable of equal conductivity for the same span, and ask which cable the pylons have to support.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A metal that conducts electricity well must also conduct heat equally well, in the same proportion.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both properties come from the same delocalised electrons, so learners assume one number ('how good a conductor') describes both without separate measurement.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner assumes the best electrical conductor is automatically also the single best thermal conductor, or treats the two rankings as identical by definition rather than checking them.
misconceptions.correct_model: Electrical and thermal conductivity in metals share the same underlying cause (free-moving delocalised electrons), so metals that are good electrical conductors also tend to be good thermal conductors, but the two properties are measured separately and are not forced to be in exactly the same order or proportion for every pair of metals.
misconceptions.remediation: State that both properties rank metals similarly for this course (good electrical conductors are also good thermal conductors) but ask the learner to say in their own words why that is a tendency from shared structure, not an exact mathematical law.

common_mistakes.mistake: Justifying a material choice with only one property when the use really depends on a trade-off between two or more.
common_mistakes.why: A single standout property (such as 'copper conducts well') is easy to recall and state, while the competing property that actually decides the trade-off is easy to overlook.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: For any 'why is metal X used for Y' question, name every property that could plausibly matter, then state which one is decisive for that specific use and why the others are not.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating 'no reaction observed in a short test' as proof that no reaction is possible.
common_mistakes.why: A short classroom observation window makes a very slow reaction look identical to no reaction at all.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State reactivity conclusions in terms of rate and conditions ('no visible reaction with cold water in a few minutes') rather than as an absolute ('never reacts').

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming all metals share every typical metallic property to the same degree.
common_mistakes.why: The general description of 'a metal' as a category blurs into a description of every individual metal.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always check a property claim against data for the specific metal named, since density, conductivity and reactivity all vary considerably between different metals.

exam_notes: When asked to explain a metal's use, name the specific property first, then explain, in terms of structure (metallic bonding, delocalised electrons, oxide layer) why that metal has that property.

When comparing two metals for the same use, state the trade-off explicitly: name both competing properties and say which one the specific use weighs more heavily, rather than naming only the winning property.
Avoid absolute words ('always', 'never', 'all metals') in reactivity or property statements unless the question itself asks for a general rule; general tendencies in this topic have real exceptions.

summary.big_idea: A metal is chosen for a job because its specific measured properties, not a vague sense of being 'a good metal', match what that job requires, and a use often depends on a trade-off between two or more properties.
key_points: Metals tend to be good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable, because of metallic bonding and delocalised electrons, but these are tendencies with real exceptions, not exception-free rules.
Reaction with cold water, steam and dilute acid is a chemical property that varies between metals in a consistent pattern, from the most reactive to the least reactive.

Aluminium's low density suits aircraft, drinks cans and overhead cables; copper's conductivity suits indoor wiring and cookware bases; the choice between similar metals is often a trade-off, not a single deciding property.
A short test showing no visible reaction only limits the rate of a possible reaction under those conditions; it does not prove a reaction is impossible.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Name the specific property a use needs, then check whether the specific metal actually has it in a high enough amount; never reason from 'it's a metal' alone.

exit_check.question: A manufacturer must choose between two metals, both with similar conductivity, for a long overhead power cable strung between pylons. One is twice as dense as the other. Which would you recommend, and why?
exit_check.answer: The less dense metal, because a long, self-supporting cable's main design constraint is usually its own weight; with similar conductivity, the lighter metal needs a smaller mass of cable to achieve the same electrical performance, reducing the load the pylons have to support and the sagging between them.

02_Alloys_improve_useful_properties.json.title: Alloys improve useful properties
02_Alloys_improve_useful_properties.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: Define an alloy as a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements, identify brass and stainless steel from their composition or from a particle diagram, and state a use for each that matches a named property.

Explain why an alloy is generally harder and stronger than the pure metal it is based on, in terms of different-sized atoms disrupting the regular layers of the metallic lattice and hindering layers from sliding over each other.

prerequisites.statement: A pure metal's atoms are arranged in regular layers that can slide over one another under force, which is why pure metals are malleable.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: The alloy-hardening explanation in this lesson is entirely about what happens when that regularity is broken, so the regular case has to be clear first.

prerequisites.statement: A mixture contains two or more substances together, in a proportion that is not fixed by a chemical formula, and no new chemical bond forms between them.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: An alloy is a specific kind of mixture (of a metal with other elements); confusing it with a compound of fixed formula is the central misconception this lesson must prevent.

diagnostic_items.question: Beaker 1 holds iron filings and powdered sulfur that have simply been stirred together. Beaker 2 holds iron(II) sulfide, $\mathrm{FeS}$, made by heating that same stirred powder strongly. State which beaker holds a mixture, and give one piece of evidence from the descriptions that supports your choice.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Beaker 1 holds the mixture. Its iron and sulfur have only been stirred together, so no new chemical bond has formed between them and the proportion of iron to sulfur could be changed freely. Beaker 2's contents have the formula $\mathrm{FeS}$, which fixes the ratio of iron to sulfur exactly, so beaker 2 holds a compound.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Beaker 2, because it contains two different elements.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner is using 'more than one element is present' as the test for a mixture, but both beakers contain iron and sulfur; the test is whether the proportions are fixed by a formula and whether new bonds have formed.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Both are mixtures, because the iron and the sulfur are both still there in each beaker.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner does not yet separate 'the same elements are present' from 'the elements are chemically combined'; heating has produced a new compound in beaker 2.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: This checks that the learner identifies a mixture by its variable, formula-free composition and the absence of new chemical bonds, rather than by how many different elements are present. That is exactly the distinction needed before an alloy can be classified correctly, which is the central misconception of this lesson.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner, for each beaker, whether the proportion of iron to sulfur could be changed and the contents still be given the same name; only the mixture allows it.

theory_blocks.title: Why mix a pure metal with something else at all?
theory_blocks.body:
Pure gold is soft enough to be scratched by a fingernail; pure iron rusts within days of being left out in the rain; pure copper, hammered into a kitchen pan, would dent under normal use far more easily than most cooks would accept.

In each case, the pure metal has a property that is a problem for a particular job.

The practical fix, known for thousands of years, is not to find a different pure metal, but to deliberately mix a small amount of one or more other elements into the metal while it is molten.

The result, once it solidifies, is an [[blue:**alloy**]]: gold mixed with a little copper or silver becomes hard enough for jewellery to survive daily wear;

iron mixed with chromium becomes stainless steel, which resists rusting; copper mixed with zinc becomes brass, harder than either pure metal and with a different, attractive colour and sound.

theory_blocks.title: An alloy is a mixture, named but not fixed
theory_blocks.body:
An **alloy** is a mixture that contains a metal together with one or more other elements (which may themselves be metals or non-metals), deliberately combined while molten so that, once solid, the different atoms are mixed throughout the structure.

Two named alloys required at this level:

- **Brass**: copper mixed with zinc. It is harder than pure copper, has a distinctive gold-like colour, and is used for door fittings, musical instruments and decorative items.
- **Stainless steel**: iron mixed with chromium (commonly also nickel and carbon). The chromium gives it resistance to rusting that plain iron or ordinary steel does not have, so it is used for cutlery (which also needs its hardness), sinks and surgical instruments.

Because an alloy is a mixture, not a compound, it has **no single fixed formula**: the exact proportion of each element can and does vary between different grades of brass or stainless steel,

each tuned for a slightly different balance of hardness, colour or corrosion resistance.

theory_blocks.title: Reading a particle diagram as pure metal or alloy
theory_blocks.body:
The two-panel figure above is also the test for recognising a structure diagram. A **pure metal** diagram shows one size and colour of circle, arranged in clean, regular rows.

An **alloy** diagram shows at least two different sizes (or two different colours representing different elements) of circle, with the rows visibly disturbed rather than perfectly regular.

Spotting 'more than one colour or size, arranged irregularly' is enough to identify a diagram as an alloy without needing to know the exact elements involved.

theory_blocks.title: Different-sized atoms jam the sliding layers
theory_blocks.body:
In a pure metal, every atom is the same size, so the lattice forms regular layers that fit together neatly, like identical balls stacked in a tray.

Under an applied force, one whole layer can slide over the next without much resistance, because every atom in the moving layer lines up with the gaps in the layer below. This is exactly why pure metals are malleable and ductile.

When an alloy is formed, atoms of a different size (larger or smaller) are scattered through the lattice among the original atoms.

These foreign atoms no longer fit the regular spacing: they bulge the surrounding layers out of their neat rows.

A layer trying to slide past its neighbour now has to force its way past these irregular bulges instead of gliding smoothly through matching gaps, which takes considerably more force.

The result is a harder, stronger material: the alloy resists being scratched, bent or deformed better than the pure metal did, precisely because its internal layers can no longer slide past each other as freely.

The added atoms may take the place of some host atoms (**substitutional** alloying, as with zinc atoms in copper to make brass) or, if they are much smaller, squeeze into the gaps between host atoms (as small carbon atoms do between iron atoms in steel).

Either way the regular rows are disrupted, so at this level the same explanation applies: different-sized atoms stop the layers sliding easily.

assets.caption: Pure metal (left): identical atoms sit in regular rows, so the slip plane between two layers stays straight and one layer slides over the next easily. Alloy (right): each larger gold atom pushes the surrounding atoms out of line, bending the rows and the slip plane, so the layers can no longer slide past each other freely.
assets.purpose: Shows the actual distortion the text describes: the host atoms around each larger atom are visibly displaced and the slip plane is bent, so a student can see why sliding is blocked instead of taking it on trust.

keywords.definition: A mixture containing a metal together with one or more other elements, with no fixed formula.
An alloy of copper and zinc, harder than pure copper, used for fittings and instruments.
An alloy of iron with chromium (often also nickel and carbon), resistant to rusting.
Alloying in which atoms of a different size take the place of host atoms within the same metallic lattice, distorting its regular rows.
The sliding of one layer of atoms over another in a metallic lattice, responsible for malleability in pure metals and hindered in most alloys.

worked_examples.statement: **Naming two alloys.** State the two elements present in brass and the main element added to iron to make stainless steel.
solution: Brass contains copper and zinc.
Stainless steel is iron with chromium added (commonly also nickel and carbon in specific grades), with the chromium responsible for its rust resistance.
worked_examples.interpretation: Naming both elements, not just the 'main' metal, is required to show the alloy is understood as a mixture of named substances rather than as a single labelled material.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining hardness from structure.** A particle diagram shows a metal lattice where most circles are one size, with several noticeably larger circles scattered through it, disturbing the regular rows. Explain why the material shown is likely harder than the pure metal made only of the smaller circles.
solution: The diagram shows two different sizes of atom mixed together, so it represents an alloy, not a pure metal.
In the pure metal alone, every atom is the same size, so the layers are regular and can slide over one another easily.

The larger atoms scattered through this structure distort the regular rows, so a layer trying to slide past its neighbour is blocked by these irregular bulges; more force is needed to deform the structure, making the alloy harder and stronger than the pure metal.
worked_examples.interpretation: This rehearses the full chain from 'diagram shows two sizes' to 'therefore harder', the exact reasoning a Supplement-level exam question expects.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stating that the alloy is harder 'because it's an alloy', without explaining the layer-slip mechanism that actually causes the hardening.

worked_examples.statement: **Testing the lubrication idea.** A student claims that mixing a second, smaller element into a pure metal should make the metal softer, 'because small particles between bigger ones should help them slide, like oil between gears.' Evaluate this claim using the layer-slip model.
solution: The lubrication analogy assumes the added atoms sit loosely between the layers and reduce friction, the way oil molecules do between separate moving metal parts.

In an alloy, however, the added atoms are not a separate loose layer: they are locked into the same rigid lattice (either replacing host atoms or squeezed into the gaps between them), distorting the shape of the rows the host atoms sit in.

Because the distortion makes the rows irregular rather than smooth, sliding becomes harder, not easier, regardless of whether the added atoms are larger or smaller than the host atoms; the lubrication analogy describes a different physical situation (separate moving surfaces) and does not apply to atoms substituted inside one continuous lattice.
worked_examples.interpretation: Directly dismantles the lubrication idea by naming exactly why that analogy fails: it describes the wrong kind of structure (separate surfaces, not a single distorted lattice).

guided_exercises.statement: Two particle diagrams are shown. Diagram P has one size of circle throughout, in neat rows. Diagram Q has mostly one size of circle, but with scattered larger circles breaking up the rows. Identify which diagram shows a pure metal and which shows an alloy, and predict which one is harder.
hints: Count how many different sizes or colours of circle appear in each diagram before deciding anything else.
A pure metal diagram should have perfectly regular rows; check whether that is true for both diagrams.
Hardness in this model comes from how easily layers can slide; look at which diagram's rows are less regular.
guided_exercises.answer: Diagram P is the pure metal, since it has only one size of circle in perfectly regular rows. Diagram Q is the alloy, since the scattered larger circles distort the regular rows. Diagram Q (the alloy) is predicted to be harder, because its distorted rows resist the layers sliding past each other more than diagram P's regular rows do.
common_errors: Assuming the diagram with more total circles, rather than the one with more than one size of circle, must be the alloy.

guided_exercises.statement: A jeweller is asked why 24-carat (pure) gold rings bend and scratch far more easily than 18-carat gold rings, which are gold alloyed with a small amount of copper and silver. Explain the difference using the layer-slip model, and state what kind of substance 18-carat gold is (compound, element or mixture).
hints: First classify 18-carat gold: does it have a fixed single formula, or a mixture of elements that can vary slightly between pieces?
Then think about what the added copper and silver atoms, being a different size from gold atoms, do to the regular layers of the gold lattice.
Connect the structural disruption directly to the everyday observation (bending and scratching) the jeweller is asking about.
guided_exercises.answer: 18-carat gold is a mixture (specifically an alloy): it contains gold together with copper and silver, in proportions that are not fixed by any chemical formula. The copper and silver atoms are a different size from gold atoms, so when mixed into the gold lattice they distort its regular rows; this makes it harder for the layers to slide past each other than in pure (24-carat) gold, so 18-carat gold resists bending and scratching considerably better than the pure metal.
common_errors: Calling 18-carat gold a compound because it has a standard, well-known name, instead of checking whether its composition is fixed by a chemical formula.

exercises.statement: Explain, in one sentence, why an alloy such as brass does not have one single fixed chemical formula, even though 'brass' is a single familiar name.
exercises.answer: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc, and the proportion of copper to zinc can be varied to produce brass with slightly different properties, so there is no single fixed ratio that a chemical formula could represent.

exercises.statement: A manufacturer of surgical instruments chooses stainless steel rather than plain (unalloyed) steel. State the property that makes this choice necessary, and name the element added to iron that is directly responsible for it.
exercises.answer: The necessary property is resistance to rusting/corrosion, since surgical instruments are repeatedly sterilised with heat and moisture and must not corrode or contaminate a wound; the element responsible is chromium, added to the iron to form stainless steel.

exercises.statement: A particle diagram shows two different sizes of circle mixed together with no regular pattern, filling the whole sample. A second particle diagram shows the same two sizes of circle, but arranged as alternating, perfectly regular rows with a fixed 1:1 ratio everywhere in the sample. Explain why only one of these two diagrams is consistent with an alloy.
exercises.answer: Only the first diagram (irregular mixing, no fixed pattern) is consistent with an alloy, because an alloy's composition and arrangement are not fixed by a chemical rule. The second diagram, with a perfectly regular, repeating 1:1 arrangement throughout the whole sample, describes a fixed-ratio, ordered structure, which is the pattern expected of a compound rather than a mixture such as an alloy.
common_errors: Assuming any diagram with two sizes of circle must automatically be an alloy, without checking whether the arrangement is a fixed, regular pattern (which would instead suggest a compound).

exercises.statement: Solder, used to join electronic components, is traditionally an alloy of tin and lead (now often tin and copper, for safety reasons). Pure tin melts at a higher, less convenient temperature for delicate electronic work than the solder alloy does. Using the idea that mixing disrupts a metal's regular lattice, suggest why alloying can also lower a metal's melting point, not only change its hardness.
exercises.answer: A pure metal's regular, repeating lattice allows every atom to settle into the same strong, well-matched arrangement, which takes a well-defined, relatively high amount of thermal energy to break apart. When a second element with differently sized atoms is mixed in, the lattice is less regular and less uniformly packed, so the overall structure is held together slightly less efficiently; less thermal energy is then needed to disrupt it enough for the solid to melt, which is why many alloys melt at a lower, and often more useful, temperature than either of their pure component metals.

exam_questions.statement: A student claims: 'Brass must be a compound, because it always behaves the same way and has one chemical name.' Evaluate this claim and give the correct classification of brass, with a reason.
exam_questions.answer: The claim is incorrect. Brass is a mixture (an alloy of copper and zinc), not a compound. Having one familiar name does not mean a substance has one fixed composition: the exact proportion of copper to zinc in brass can be varied by the manufacturer to adjust hardness and colour, which is not possible for a true compound, whose formula fixes the ratio of its elements exactly. 'Behaving consistently' in everyday use reflects that manufacturers keep the proportions within a similar range for a given product, not that the ratio is fixed by a chemical law.
mark_scheme: States that the claim is incorrect / brass is not a compound.
States that brass is a mixture (an alloy of copper and zinc).
Explains that the copper:zinc ratio in brass is variable, not fixed.
Explains why having a single familiar name does not imply a fixed composition.

exam_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of the arrangement of atoms, why alloying a pure metal with a different-sized element generally makes the metal harder and stronger, and explain why this means an alloy is also usually less malleable than the pure metal it is based on.
exam_questions.answer: In the pure metal, all atoms are the same size and pack into regular layers that can slide smoothly over each other under an applied force, which is what makes the pure metal malleable. When atoms of a different size are mixed in to form the alloy, they distort these regular layers, creating irregular bulges that block layers from sliding past each other as freely. Because more force is now needed to make the layers move at all, the alloy resists being permanently deformed, which is observed as increased hardness and strength. Since malleability is itself the ability of layers to slide and reshape under force, and the alloy's layers are now harder to slide, the same structural change that increases hardness also reduces malleability: the alloy is less easily hammered into new shapes than the pure metal was.
mark_scheme: States that pure metal atoms are the same size and form regular, easily-sliding layers.
States that differently sized atoms distort these regular layers in an alloy.
Explains that the distortion blocks/hinders layers sliding past each other.
Links the hindered sliding to increased hardness and strength.
Explicitly connects reduced ease of sliding to reduced malleability, not just restating hardness.

challenge_questions.statement:
**Reading alloy data.** A metallurgist measures three samples: pure copper, and two brasses containing different amounts of zinc.

| Sample | Zinc content / % | Approximate melting point / °C | Approximate Brinell hardness |
|---|---|---|---|
| pure copper | 0 | 1085 | 40 |
| brass A | 20 | 1000 | 60 |
| brass B | 40 | 900 | 90 |

(a) Describe, in one sentence each, how hardness and how melting point change as the zinc content increases.
(b) A student says: *'Brass B must be the hardest because it has the highest melting point, and a higher melting point always means the atoms are held together more strongly.'* Use the data to show that this reasoning fails, then give the correct structural explanation for brass B's hardness.
(c) A manufacturer wants an alloy that sets harder than pure copper but that can be melted and poured into moulds using as little heating as possible. State which sample they should choose, and justify it with two numbers from the table.
hints: For (a), read each column downwards in turn and say simply whether the numbers rise or fall as the zinc content rises.
For (b), test the student's claim against the melting-point column before explaining anything else.
For the structural part of (b), use the layer-slip model: what do differently sized atoms do to the regular rows?
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) Hardness increases as the zinc content increases: 40, then 60, then 90. Melting point decreases as the zinc content increases: 1085 °C, then 1000 °C, then 900 °C.

(b) The student's claim fails on the data itself: brass B is indeed the hardest, but it has the **lowest** melting point of the three (900 °C), not the highest, so in this set hardness and melting point move in opposite directions and one cannot be used to explain the other. Brass B is hardest because zinc atoms are a different size from copper atoms and are mixed throughout the lattice, distorting its regular rows so that the layers can no longer slide over one another easily; hardness here comes from blocked layer slip, not from a raised melting point. The same loss of regular packing is also why the alloy melts at a lower temperature than pure copper.

(c) Brass B. It is the hardest of the three (Brinell hardness 90, against 40 for pure copper) and it has the lowest melting point (900 °C, against 1085 °C for pure copper), so it needs the least heating to melt and pour yet still sets much harder than the pure metal.
common_errors: Accepting the student's claim in (b) because 'harder' sounds like 'stronger bonds', without checking the melting-point column that contradicts it.
Describing brass B as harder simply 'because it is an alloy', without naming the different-sized atoms and the blocked layer slip.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly describes brass?

options.text: A compound of copper and zinc in a fixed 1:1 ratio
options.why_wrong: brass has no fixed formula ratio; its copper:zinc proportion can be varied, which rules out 'compound'.

options.text: A pure element found naturally in this exact form
options.why_wrong: brass contains two different elements and is manufactured, not a single pure element.

options.text: A mixture (alloy) of copper and zinc, in a proportion that can be varied
Iron alloyed with chromium
options.why_wrong: this describes stainless steel, not brass; brass contains copper and zinc.

mcq.explanation: Brass is an alloy (a mixture) of copper and zinc; the proportion of each element is not fixed by a chemical formula and can be adjusted to change the alloy's properties.

mcq.stem: A particle diagram shows one size of circle arranged in perfectly regular, repeating rows throughout the whole sample. What does this diagram most likely represent?

options.text: An alloy
options.why_wrong: an alloy diagram needs at least two different sizes or colours of atom; only one size is shown here.

options.text: A compound of two elements
options.why_wrong: a compound requires at least two different elements chemically bonded; only one type of circle is shown.

options.text: A mixture of two metals
options.why_wrong: a mixture of two metals (an alloy) would show two different sizes or colours of circle, not one.

options.text: A pure metal

mcq.explanation: One size of atom in perfectly regular rows is exactly the structure expected of a pure metal; a second, differently sized atom disrupting the rows would be needed to show an alloy instead.

mcq.stem: Why does mixing a different-sized element into a pure metal usually make it harder, rather than softer?

options.text: The added atoms distort the regular layers, making it harder for layers to slide past each other
The added atoms act as a lubricant, letting layers slide more freely
options.why_wrong: this is the opposite of what actually happens; the added atoms distort the lattice and hinder sliding, they do not lubricate it.

options.text: The added atoms form new, stronger chemical bonds between every pair of neighbouring atoms
options.why_wrong: alloying does not create new chemical bonds between the mixed atoms; the metallic bonding itself is not fundamentally changed, only the regularity of the packing is.

options.text: The added atoms increase the overall density of the metal, which always increases hardness
options.why_wrong: density change is not the mechanism taught for alloy hardening, and higher density does not by itself guarantee greater hardness.

mcq.explanation: Different-sized atoms disrupt the regular rows of the lattice, so layers can no longer slide past each other as smoothly as in the pure metal, which is observed as increased hardness and strength.

mcq.stem: Which pair correctly matches an alloy with the element mainly responsible for the named property?

options.text: Brass; chromium gives its gold-like colour
options.why_wrong: brass contains copper and zinc, not chromium; chromium is the key added element in stainless steel, not brass.

options.text: Stainless steel; chromium gives rust resistance
Stainless steel; carbon alone gives complete rust resistance
options.why_wrong: the rust resistance of stainless steel is mainly due to chromium, not carbon; plain carbon steel (iron and carbon, without chromium) still rusts.

options.text: Brass; zinc gives it the ability to conduct electricity for the first time
options.why_wrong: copper alone already conducts electricity very well; zinc is not what gives brass the ability to conduct, since pure copper already does.

mcq.explanation: Stainless steel is iron alloyed with chromium (often with nickel and carbon too); it is specifically the chromium that gives stainless steel its resistance to rusting.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: An alloy is a compound with a fixed chemical formula, like a compound of fixed-ratio elements.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Alloys have fixed-sounding names (brass, stainless steel, bronze) that look like the names of pure substances, so learners assume a single fixed composition must lie behind the name.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner writes or expects a chemical formula for brass or stainless steel, or insists all brass must contain exactly the same percentage of zinc.
misconceptions.correct_model: An alloy is a mixture, not a compound: brass can be made with different proportions of copper and zinc depending on the properties wanted, and stainless steel's exact mix of iron, chromium, nickel and carbon varies between grades, with no single fixed ratio required by a chemical law.
misconceptions.remediation: Show two samples described as 'brass' with different stated copper:zinc percentages and ask whether both can still correctly be called brass.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Atoms of different sizes mixed together make it easier for layers to slide past each other.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners may picture smaller atoms as acting like a lubricant between larger ones, by analogy with everyday lubrication, rather than picturing the irregular packing that actually results.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that an alloy will be softer or more malleable than the pure metal, or explains hardening using a 'lubrication' analogy.
misconceptions.correct_model: Different-sized atoms distort the regular rows of the lattice, so the layers no longer line up neatly; this irregularity makes it harder, not easier, for layers to slide past one another, which is why alloys are typically harder and stronger than the pure metal alone.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare the two-panel diagram of a pure metal (regular rows, easy slip) with an alloy (irregular packing, hindered slip) and ask which arrangement looks easier to slide, pointing at the actual disruption rather than relying on the lubrication analogy.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Stainless steel is pure iron, perhaps just given a shinier surface treatment.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Stainless steel looks and feels like a single uniform grey metal, with no visible second colour the way a copper-and-zinc alloy sometimes shows a different shade, so learners assume no other element is really present.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes stainless steel as 'iron that doesn't rust' without naming the other elements responsible, or denies that stainless steel is an alloy at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with chromium (and often nickel and carbon); it is the added chromium that gives stainless steel its resistance to rusting, by forming a thin protective oxide layer, and without that added chromium the iron underneath would rust just like ordinary iron.
misconceptions.remediation: Name the actual composition (iron plus chromium, often with nickel and carbon) and ask what would happen to a chromium-free iron object left in damp air, to connect the added element directly to the named property.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating an alloy as a compound with a fixed formula because it has a single familiar name.
common_mistakes.why: Names like 'brass' or 'stainless steel' sound like the name of one pure substance, hiding that the underlying composition can vary.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Ask whether the exact proportion of elements is fixed by a chemical rule or can be deliberately varied; if it can vary, it is a mixture, however consistent the name sounds.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining alloy hardness with a 'lubrication' idea, where smaller particles are imagined to help layers slide.
common_mistakes.why: The everyday idea of lubrication (something small helping big things slide) is intuitive but describes a different physical situation (separate moving surfaces, not atoms substituted inside one lattice).
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always describe the mechanism as 'different-sized atoms distort the regular rows and hinder sliding', the opposite of lubrication, and check this against the two-panel diagram.

common_mistakes.mistake: Naming only the 'main' metal in an alloy (for example, calling stainless steel 'a type of iron') without naming the added element responsible for its special property.
common_mistakes.why: The base metal is the larger, more familiar component, so the smaller added element is easy to leave out.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name both (or all) elements present and state explicitly which one is responsible for the property being discussed.

exam_notes: State explicitly that an alloy is a mixture, not a compound, whenever asked to classify brass, stainless steel, or any other named alloy.

When explaining hardness, always complete the full chain: different-sized atoms -> distorted regular rows -> layers cannot slide as easily -> harder/stronger material; a partial chain ('it's harder because it's mixed') will not gain full credit.
When asked for a property/use pairing, name the specific added element responsible (chromium for stainless steel's rust resistance), not just the alloy's name.

summary.big_idea: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements; mixing in different-sized atoms distorts the metal's regular layers and hinders them from sliding, making the alloy generally harder and stronger than the pure metal.
key_points: An alloy is a mixture, not a compound: it has no fixed formula, and its composition can be deliberately varied.
Brass is copper alloyed with zinc; stainless steel is iron alloyed with chromium (often with nickel and carbon), which is specifically responsible for its rust resistance.
A pure metal's regular rows of identical atoms slide past each other easily; an alloy's different-sized atoms distort these rows and hinder sliding.
A structure diagram shows a pure metal as one size/colour of atom in regular rows, and an alloy as at least two sizes/colours with the rows disturbed.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Alloying mixes in different-sized atoms, which distort the metal's regular layers and make sliding harder, so the alloy comes out harder and stronger than the pure metal.

exit_check.question: A diagram shows a metal lattice with two sizes of atom, scattered with no fixed repeating pattern. A student says this must be a compound because it contains two elements. Is the student correct?
exit_check.answer: No. A compound requires a fixed, regular ratio of chemically bonded elements. Two sizes of atom scattered with no fixed pattern, and no indication of chemical bonding between them, describes a mixture, specifically an alloy, not a compound.
