theory_blocks.title: Reading reactivity from a race, not from a list
theory_blocks.body:
Imagine strips of five different metals, each dropped into its own beaker of dilute hydrochloric acid at the same moment. One strip bubbles so fast the beaker nearly overflows with gas;

another bubbles steadily but much more gently; a third produces barely a trickle of bubbles over several minutes; a fourth and fifth produce nothing visible at all, even after a long wait.

Before any list of metals is memorised, this single observation already gives real information: [[green:the metal that reacted fastest is the most reactive of the five]], and [[red:the metals that produced nothing are the least reactive]].

A reactivity series is nothing more than this race, repeated and recorded carefully with cold water, steam and dilute acid, for a standard set of metals, and then written down in order from fastest/most vigorous to slowest/no reaction.

theory_blocks.title: Three tests, three thresholds, one order
theory_blocks.body:
Three separate tests mark out different thresholds of reactivity, and a metal's position in the series is read from exactly which of the three tests it still reacts with:

- **Cold water**: only the most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium) react visibly, producing the metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
- **Steam**: metals too unreactive for cold water, but still reactive enough for a hotter, more energetic test, react here instead (magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron), producing the metal oxide and hydrogen gas.
- **Dilute acid**: this is the most sensitive test of the three. Every metal that reacted with cold water or steam also reacts with dilute acid, and in addition, the speed of bubbling ranks the metals in the middle of the series (magnesium fizzes vigorously, zinc steadily, iron slowly). Every metal above hydrogen in the series reacts with dilute acid, giving a salt and hydrogen gas; copper, silver and gold, below hydrogen, do not.

The full stated series, built from exactly this evidence and placing carbon and hydrogen in as reference points rather than as metals, runs from most to least reactive: **potassium,

sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold**.

assets.caption: The reactivity series as a ladder, with each metal's reaction with cold water, steam and dilute acid: green = vigorous or clear reaction, gold = slower or moderate reaction, red = no reaction. Carbon and hydrogen are greyed out across all three columns because they are reference points, not metals, so these tests do not apply to them.
assets.purpose: Lets a learner read a metal's series position directly off the pattern of its three reaction results, and makes the 'no reaction with water but reacts with acid' pattern (zinc, iron) visually explicit, without claiming results for the two non-metal reference points.

theory_blocks.title: Writing the equations for these reactions
theory_blocks.body:
Each of the three tests has its own standard pattern of products, and both the word equation and the balanced symbol equation are expected.

**The most reactive metals with cold water** give the metal **hydroxide** and hydrogen:

sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen

$2\mathrm{Na} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

calcium + water → calcium hydroxide + hydrogen

$\mathrm{Ca} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

Potassium follows sodium's pattern exactly: $2\mathrm{K} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$.

**Metals with steam** give the metal **oxide** and hydrogen, because at this higher temperature the water supplies only its oxygen to the metal:

magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen

$\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgO} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

zinc + steam → zinc oxide + hydrogen

$\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnO} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

**Metals with dilute acid** give a salt and hydrogen:

zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen

$\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

iron + hydrochloric acid → iron(II) chloride + hydrogen

$\mathrm{Fe} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$

[[blue:The one difference worth memorising is hydroxide from cold water, oxide from steam]]; hydrogen gas is released in all three cases. Finish every equation by counting atoms on each side: in $\mathrm{Ca} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OH)_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$, for example, there is 1 Ca, 4 H and 2 O on each side.

theory_blocks.title: Carbon and hydrogen: markers, not metals
theory_blocks.body:
Carbon and hydrogen sit inside the series purely as **reference points**. Neither is a metal: carbon does not conduct electricity like a metal (except as graphite, for a different reason) and is not malleable, and hydrogen is a gas with none of the general metallic properties.

[[blue:They earn a place in the sequence because comparing a metal's position with carbon's tells you directly whether carbon can be used to extract that metal from its ore by reduction]] (developed fully in lesson 5), and comparing with hydrogen shows whether a metal reacts with dilute acid (metals above hydrogen do; copper, silver and gold, below it, do not).

Treat 'where does carbon sit' and 'where does hydrogen sit' as two fixed landmarks on the same ladder, never as two more metals to rank.

theory_blocks.title: Reactivity is how readily a metal loses electrons
theory_blocks.body:
The underlying reason one metal outreacts another is that reactivity, for a metal, is the tendency of its atoms to **lose electrons and form positive ions**. A metal higher in the series loses electrons more readily than a metal lower in the series.

For example, $\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-$ happens more readily than $\mathrm{Cu} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^-$, because zinc is higher in the series than copper.

This single idea explains every reaction pattern seen so far: a metal reacting with water, steam or acid is losing electrons to form its positive ion while hydrogen ions gain electrons to form hydrogen gas,

so 'more reactive' and 'loses electrons more readily' are two descriptions of exactly the same underlying tendency, not two separate facts to memorise.

theory_blocks.title: Predicting a displacement reaction
theory_blocks.body:
A **displacement reaction** happens when a metal is added to an aqueous solution of a compound of a different metal, and the added metal is more reactive (higher in the series) than the metal already combined in the compound.

The more reactive metal loses its electrons to become the dissolved ion, while the less reactive metal's ions gain electrons and come out of solution as the solid metal.

**Rule, in three steps:** (1) find both metals' positions in the series; (2) if the added metal is higher (more reactive), displacement occurs: the added metal replaces the other metal in the compound, and the displaced metal comes out of solution as a solid; (3) if the added metal is lower (less reactive), no reaction occurs, and nothing should be written beyond 'no reaction'.

Example: zinc added to copper sulfate solution. Zinc is higher in the series than copper, so zinc displaces copper: $\mathrm{Zn} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$.

Checked atom by atom: one zinc, one copper and one sulfate group appear on each side, so the equation is balanced. The domain of this rule is strictly aqueous metal-compound solutions reacting with a solid metal from this series;

it does not, by itself, predict reactions with non-metal compounds or reactions outside aqueous solution.

keywords.definition: An ordered list of metals (with carbon and hydrogen as reference points) from most to least reactive, built from their reactions with water, steam and dilute acid.
A reaction in which a more reactive metal takes the place of a less reactive metal in an aqueous compound, releasing the less reactive metal as a solid.
A non-metal (carbon or hydrogen) placed in the reactivity series purely for comparison, not because it is itself a metal.
The loss of electrons by an atom or ion, forming a more positively charged species; this is what happens to the more reactive metal in a displacement reaction.
The gain of electrons by an atom or ion, forming a less positively charged species; this is what happens to the less reactive metal's ions in a displacement reaction.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the ladder.** Using the reactivity ladder, state whether iron reacts with (a) cold water, (b) steam, (c) dilute acid.
solution: (a) No reaction: iron sits below the metals that react with cold water (potassium, sodium, calcium).
(b) Reacts: iron is among the metals (magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron) that react with steam, though more slowly than zinc.
(c) Reacts: iron reacts with dilute acid, producing iron(II) chloride (or another iron salt, depending on the acid) and hydrogen gas.
worked_examples.interpretation: This rehearses reading three separate results for one metal, directly targeting the assumption that a 'no' result with cold water also means 'no' with dilute acid.

worked_examples.statement: **Predicting a displacement reaction.** Predict what happens when a strip of iron is placed in copper sulfate solution. Write a balanced equation if a reaction occurs, and check it is balanced.
solution: Find both metals' positions: iron is higher (more reactive) than copper in the series.

Because the added metal (iron) is more reactive than the metal in the compound (copper), displacement occurs: iron goes into solution as iron ions, and copper comes out of solution as solid copper (observations: the blue colour of the solution fades and a pink-brown coating of copper forms on the iron).
Equation: $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$.
Check: one iron, one copper and one sulfate group ($\mathrm{SO_{4}}$) appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.
worked_examples.interpretation: Following the three-step rule explicitly, including the atom-balance check, models the full expected working for any displacement prediction.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Writing the correct word description but an unbalanced or wrongly-charged formula, such as FeSO4 written as Fe2SO4.

worked_examples.statement: **An unfamiliar metal, X.** A technician tests an unknown metal X: X shows no reaction with cold water, reacts with steam, and reacts with dilute acid, bubbling more vigorously than iron does under the same conditions but less vigorously than magnesium. Place X in the series relative to magnesium, aluminium and iron, and predict whether X would displace iron from iron(II) sulfate solution.
solution: No reaction with cold water, but reaction with steam, places X in the magnesium-to-iron band of the series (above copper, which does not react with steam, and below the metals that react with cold water).

X bubbles more vigorously with dilute acid than iron, so X is more reactive than iron; X bubbles less vigorously than magnesium, so X is less reactive than magnesium. This places X between magnesium and iron, consistent with (though not proving) a position close to aluminium or zinc.
Because X is more reactive than iron, X would displace iron from iron(II) sulfate solution, producing a sulfate of X and solid iron.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Trying to name metal X exactly, when the question only requires placing it relative to named metals and predicting one displacement outcome from that relative position.

guided_exercises.statement: A student is given four unlabelled metal strips and dilute acid only (no water or steam available). Explain why dilute acid alone cannot always tell the four metals apart, even though it is the most sensitive of the three tests, and suggest what extra test would help.
hints: Think about which section of the series dilute acid actually distinguishes: does every reactive metal in this range bubble at a visibly different rate, or could two metals seem similar?
Consider two metals close together in the series, such as magnesium and aluminium, or zinc and iron: would their acid-bubbling rates necessarily look clearly different by eye alone?
The extra test should use a different threshold (a different point at which reaction starts or stops) to separate metals that look similar in the acid test.
guided_exercises.answer: Dilute acid shows a reaction for every metal in the series except copper, silver and gold, so two metals reasonably close together in reactivity (for example magnesium and aluminium) can both bubble, and judging 'which bubbled a bit faster' by eye alone is unreliable. Adding the cold water test helps separate out the most reactive metals immediately (only potassium, sodium and calcium react with cold water), and the steam test adds a second, different threshold; using all three tests together, not acid alone, is what actually pins down a precise position in the series.
common_errors: Assuming any single test, however sensitive, can fully separate every metal in the series; each test only marks one threshold, not the whole order.

guided_exercises.statement: Predict whether a reaction occurs when a piece of silver is placed in copper sulfate solution. Explain your reasoning and state what you would actually observe.
hints: Find both metals' positions in the series first, exactly as in the three-step displacement rule.
Compare: is the added metal (silver) higher or lower in the series than the metal in the compound (copper)?
If the rule says no reaction, state plainly what would be observed, rather than leaving the answer incomplete.
guided_exercises.answer: No reaction occurs. Silver is lower in the series than copper (silver is less reactive), and the three-step rule requires the added metal to be more reactive than the metal in the compound for displacement to happen. Since silver is less reactive, it cannot displace copper from copper sulfate; the solution would stay blue and the silver strip would remain unchanged, with no solid deposit forming on it.
common_errors: Assuming that because silver and copper are both unreactive with water/acid, 'nothing happens anywhere', rather than correctly identifying that no displacement happens because of the specific relative order of these two metals.

exercises.statement: Using the series, predict whether each pair reacts, and if so, write the balanced equation: (a) magnesium added to zinc sulfate solution, (b) magnesium added to copper sulfate solution.
exercises.answer: (a) Magnesium is more reactive than zinc, so a reaction occurs: $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Zn}$ (checked: one Mg, one Zn and one sulfate group on each side). (b) Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so a reaction occurs: $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$ (checked: one Mg, one Cu and one sulfate group on each side).

exercises.statement: Explain why carbon is included in the reactivity series even though it is not a metal, and state the one practical question its position in the series answers.
exercises.answer: Carbon is included strictly as a reference point for comparing metals' reactivity, not as a metal itself, since it lacks the general properties of metals (such as conductivity and malleability). Its position answers the practical question of which metals can be extracted from their ores by reduction using carbon: metals below carbon in the series can be extracted this way, while metals above carbon cannot, because carbon is not reactive enough to remove oxygen from their more strongly held compounds.

exercises.statement: Two beakers of dilute hydrochloric acid each receive a strip of metal: beaker 1 bubbles vigorously immediately, beaker 2 shows only a faint trickle of bubbles after a minute. Beaker 1 contains either magnesium or copper; beaker 2 contains either iron or silver. Identify the metal in each beaker, with a reason for each.
exercises.answer: Beaker 1 contains magnesium: of the two possible metals, only magnesium reacts with dilute acid (copper does not react with dilute acid at all, so it could not have produced vigorous bubbling). Beaker 2 contains iron: of the two possible metals, only iron reacts with dilute acid (silver does not react with dilute acid), and iron's reaction is visibly slower than magnesium's, matching the faint trickle described.
common_errors: Picking copper or silver for either beaker because 'some reaction was seen', without checking that copper and silver do not react with dilute acid at all.

exercises.statement: Write a word equation and a balanced symbol equation for each of these reactions: (a) potassium with cold water, (b) magnesium with steam, (c) zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid.
exercises.answer: (a) potassium + water → potassium hydroxide + hydrogen; $2\mathrm{K} + 2\mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KOH} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$ (checked: 2 K, 4 H and 2 O on each side). (b) magnesium + steam → magnesium oxide + hydrogen; $\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{H_{2}O} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgO} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$ (checked: 1 Mg, 2 H and 1 O on each side). (c) zinc + hydrochloric acid → zinc chloride + hydrogen; $\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{ZnCl_{2}} + \mathrm{H_{2}}$ (checked: 1 Zn, 2 H and 2 Cl on each side).
common_errors: Writing the metal hydroxide for the steam reaction; steam gives the metal oxide, and only cold water gives the hydroxide.

exercises.statement: A recycling plant wants to recover silver from a waste solution of silver nitrate without using electricity. Suggest a metal from the series that could be added to the solution to recover solid silver, explain why your choice works, and explain why copper, specifically, would be a sensible practical choice rather than, say, potassium.
exercises.answer: Any metal more reactive than silver would work in principle (for example copper, iron or zinc), because a more reactive metal displaces silver from silver nitrate solution, depositing solid silver while the added metal's ions go into solution: for copper, $\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{AgNO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu(NO_{3})_{2}} + 2\mathrm{Ag}$ (checked: one Cu, two Ag, two N and six O on each side). Copper is a sensible practical choice because it is far enough above silver in the series to displace it reliably, but it is not so reactive that it would react dangerously with water or produce an unsafe, uncontrollable reaction; a metal like potassium is so reactive that it would react violently with any water present in the solution itself, long before it ever reached the silver ions, making it impractical and hazardous for this purpose.

exam_questions.statement: A student adds a strip of lead to a solution of tin(II) chloride and observes no reaction. In a separate test, the student adds a strip of tin to a solution of lead(II) nitrate and observes a grey solid forming on the tin strip. Using this evidence alone, state which of lead and tin is more reactive, explain your reasoning fully, and predict what the grey solid is.
exam_questions.answer: Tin is more reactive than lead. In the first test, lead added to tin(II) chloride produces no reaction, which means lead cannot displace tin from its compound, consistent with lead being the less reactive of the two. In the second test, tin added to lead(II) chloride produces a visible change (a grey solid forming), consistent with tin displacing lead from its compound, which only happens if tin is more reactive than lead. Both observations agree with the same conclusion, so the evidence is consistent. The grey solid forming on the tin strip is solid lead, deposited as tin's more readily lost electrons reduce the dissolved lead ions back to the metal.
mark_scheme: States that tin is more reactive than lead.
Explains that no reaction (lead in tin chloride) shows lead cannot displace tin.
Explains that a visible change (tin in lead chloride) shows tin can displace lead.
States that the two observations are consistent with each other, not contradictory.
Correctly identifies the grey solid as lead.

exam_questions.statement: Explain, in terms of electrons, why zinc displaces copper from copper sulfate solution, but copper does not displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution.
exam_questions.answer: Zinc is more reactive than copper, which at the level of electrons means zinc atoms lose their electrons more readily than copper atoms do. When zinc is added to copper sulfate solution, zinc atoms lose electrons to form zinc ions ($\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-$), and these electrons are gained by the dissolved copper ions, which are reduced to solid copper ($\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 2e^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Cu}$); overall, electrons pass from zinc to copper ions. For copper added to zinc sulfate solution, the reverse transfer would be needed, with copper losing electrons to zinc ions, but copper does not lose its electrons as readily as zinc does, so this electron transfer does not happen, and no reaction is observed.
mark_scheme: States that zinc is more reactive than copper / loses electrons more readily.
Gives the correct half-equation (or equivalent description) for zinc losing electrons.
Gives the correct half-equation (or equivalent description) for copper ions gaining electrons.
Explains that the reverse electron transfer (copper to zinc ions) does not happen because copper does not lose electrons as readily as zinc.

challenge_questions.statement: A sealed, unlabelled container holds a grey metal. Tests show: the metal does not react with cold water; it reacts slowly with steam, producing hydrogen gas; it reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid, more vigorously than iron does under the same conditions but less vigorously than magnesium. A second, separate test shows that this metal, when added to a solution of zinc sulfate, produces no visible change. Use all the evidence together to place this metal as precisely as the given series allows, explaining any evidence that narrows the range further than the acid test alone would.
hints: The water/steam/acid pattern alone places the metal somewhere in the magnesium-to-iron band, since it reacts with steam but not cold water.
The acid-vigour comparison (more than iron, less than magnesium) narrows this further within that band.
The zinc sulfate test adds one more constraint: think about what 'no visible change' when added to zinc sulfate actually rules out, given the three-step displacement rule.
challenge_questions.answer: From the water/steam/acid pattern, the metal reacts with steam but not cold water, which places it in the magnesium-to-iron band of the series (more reactive than copper, less reactive than the cold-water-reactive metals). The acid-vigour comparison narrows this to somewhere strictly between magnesium and iron. The zinc sulfate test adds a crucial extra constraint: no reaction with zinc sulfate means the metal cannot be more reactive than zinc (otherwise it would have displaced the zinc), so the metal must sit at or below zinc's position. Combining all three pieces of evidence, the metal's position is narrowed to between zinc and iron (more reactive than iron, but not more reactive than zinc), the tightest range the given evidence supports; the series itself places aluminium above this band, so the metal is not aluminium either.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Step 1 (water/steam/acid band): reacts with steam, not cold water -> lies between the cold-water-reactive metals and copper, i.e. within {magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron} in this series. Step 2 (acid vigour): more vigorous than iron, less vigorous than magnesium -> excludes magnesium and iron themselves as the exact identity (the metal is reactive enough to beat iron but not magnesium), leaving aluminium or zinc as the only candidates from this specific series' named entries, bearing in mind unnamed metals could also fit the same band in principle. Step 3 (zinc sulfate test): no displacement of zinc means the metal is not more reactive than zinc, which rules out any candidate more reactive than zinc, consistent with (though not uniquely proving) zinc itself or a metal just below it. Taken together, the tightest statement the evidence supports is: more reactive than iron, no more reactive than zinc, i.e. the metal's position is pinned to the zinc-to-iron region of the series, which is as precise as this evidence allows without a direct comparison against zinc and iron individually in the acid test.
common_errors: Trying to name a single unique metal from the evidence given, when the task explicitly asks only for the tightest range the evidence supports.
Ignoring the zinc sulfate result and relying on the acid-vigour comparison alone, missing the extra constraint it adds.

mcq.stem: Which metal reacts with dilute acid but shows no visible reaction with cold water?

options.text: Potassium
options.why_wrong: potassium is among the most reactive metals and reacts vigorously with cold water itself.

options.text: Copper
options.why_wrong: copper does not react with dilute acid either, so it does not fit the pattern described.

options.text: Zinc
Calcium
options.why_wrong: calcium reacts visibly with cold water, so it does not fit a metal that shows no reaction with cold water.

mcq.explanation: Zinc shows no visible reaction with cold water but reacts with dilute acid, placing it in the magnesium-to-iron band of the series, below the cold-water-reactive metals and above copper.

mcq.stem: A strip of copper is placed in zinc sulfate solution. What is observed?

options.text: The copper displaces the zinc, producing copper sulfate and solid zinc.
options.why_wrong: this reverses the correct direction; copper is less reactive than zinc, so copper cannot displace zinc.

options.text: Both metals react together to form a new alloy in the solution.
options.why_wrong: displacement reactions in aqueous solution produce a dissolved salt and a solid metal, not an alloy forming inside the solution.

options.text: The solution turns a different colour but no solid forms.
options.why_wrong: with no reaction occurring at all, there is no chemical change to the solution's composition, so no colour change would be expected either.

options.text: No reaction occurs, because copper is less reactive than zinc.

mcq.explanation: Displacement requires the added metal to be more reactive than the metal in the compound; copper is less reactive than zinc, so no reaction occurs.

mcq.stem: Why are carbon and hydrogen included in the reactivity series even though neither is a metal?

options.text: Because they act as reference points for extraction methods and acid-reaction behaviour
Because they are the two most reactive substances known
options.why_wrong: carbon and hydrogen sit in the middle/lower part of this series, not at the top; this is not the reason they are included.

options.text: Because every series must contain exactly two non-metals by convention
options.why_wrong: there is no such fixed convention; carbon and hydrogen are included for a specific, stated reason, not an arbitrary rule.

options.text: Because they are impurities commonly found in all metal ores
options.why_wrong: this is not why they appear in the series; their role is as comparison markers for reactivity, not as described impurities.

mcq.explanation: Carbon's position shows which metals can be extracted from their ores by carbon reduction, and hydrogen's position connects the series to the acid-reaction pattern used to build it; neither is a metal.

mcq.stem: Which equation correctly represents a displacement reaction that actually occurs, based on the series?

options.text: $\mathrm{Ag} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag_{2}SO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$
options.why_wrong: silver is less reactive than copper, so silver cannot displace copper from copper sulfate; this reaction does not occur.

options.text: $\mathrm{Fe} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{FeSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$
$\mathrm{Au} + \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{AuSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Cu}$
options.why_wrong: gold is far less reactive than copper, so gold cannot displace copper from copper sulfate; this reaction does not occur.

options.text: $\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{ZnSO_{4}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}} + \mathrm{Zn}$
options.why_wrong: copper is less reactive than zinc, so copper cannot displace zinc from zinc sulfate; this reaction does not occur.

mcq.explanation: Iron is more reactive than copper, so iron correctly displaces copper from copper sulfate solution, and the equation is balanced (one Fe, one Cu, one sulfate group on each side).

flashcards.front: State the reactivity series used in this course, from most to least reactive.
flashcards.back: Potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold.

flashcards.front: What does it mean for a metal to be 'reactive', at the level of electrons?
flashcards.back: A tendency for its atoms to lose electrons readily and form positive ions.

flashcards.front: Zinc shows no reaction with cold water. Does this mean zinc also shows no reaction with dilute acid?
flashcards.back: No. Zinc reacts clearly with dilute acid even though it does not react with cold water; the three tests mark different thresholds and must be checked separately.

flashcards.front: In a displacement reaction, which metal ends up as the dissolved ion: the more reactive or the less reactive one?
flashcards.back: The more reactive metal ends up as the dissolved ion; the less reactive metal's ions are reduced to the solid metal.

flashcards.front: Would iron displace silver from silver nitrate solution?
flashcards.back: Yes: iron is more reactive than silver, so iron displaces silver, forming an iron salt and solid silver.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: The less reactive metal displaces the more reactive metal from its compound.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes remember 'displacement happens' without a clear direction, and may default to whichever metal is named first in the question, or to the metal that is solid (versus dissolved) at the start.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that copper placed in zinc sulfate solution will displace the zinc, producing copper sulfate and zinc metal.
misconceptions.correct_model: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound, because the more reactive metal loses its electrons more readily, reducing the less reactive metal's ions back to the metal while itself becoming the ion in solution. Copper is less reactive than zinc, so copper placed in zinc sulfate solution produces no reaction at all.
misconceptions.remediation: Before predicting any displacement reaction, require the learner to state which of the two metals is higher in the series first, then predict the direction from that, rather than guessing from the order the metals are named in the question.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Carbon and hydrogen are metals and belong in the reactivity series in the same sense as the named metals.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Carbon and hydrogen are written into the same single sequence as the metals, in the same list format, which can make them look like just two more entries of the same kind.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes carbon or hydrogen as 'a metal' or expects carbon to form a simple positive ion and react with dilute acid the way zinc does.
misconceptions.correct_model: Carbon and hydrogen are non-metals included in the series purely as reference points, because comparing a metal's reactivity with carbon tells you directly whether that metal can be extracted from its ore using carbon as a reducing agent, and comparing with hydrogen connects to the acid-reaction pattern; neither carbon nor hydrogen is a metal, and neither undergoes the same ion-forming reactions the metals in the series do.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to state the general metallic properties (conductivity, malleability) and check that carbon and hydrogen do not have them, before placing them back into the series strictly as comparison markers.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: If a metal shows no reaction with cold water, it must also show no reaction with dilute acid.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Both tests are introduced together as 'reactivity tests', so learners may treat a 'no' result on one test as if it transfers automatically to the other, rather than checking the acid result separately.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner concludes that zinc or iron, having shown no reaction with cold water, will also show no reaction with dilute acid.
misconceptions.correct_model: Cold water, steam and dilute acid are three separate tests that become positive at three different points going down the series: a metal can easily be unreactive with cold water while still reacting clearly with dilute acid (zinc and iron are the clearest examples), so each test must be checked on its own evidence, not inferred from another test.
misconceptions.remediation: Build the comparison table/ladder explicitly with three separate columns for cold water, steam and dilute acid, and point to zinc and iron's row as the case where the water column reads 'no reaction' but the acid column reads 'reacts'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Predicting displacement in the wrong direction (the less reactive metal 'displacing' the more reactive one).
common_mistakes.why: Without first explicitly comparing series positions, it is easy to default to whichever metal happens to be named first in the question.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state both metals' series positions before predicting anything, then apply the rule: only the more reactive metal can displace the other.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming a 'no reaction' result with cold water also means 'no reaction' with dilute acid.
common_mistakes.why: Both are introduced together as reactivity tests, which can blur the fact that they mark different, separate thresholds.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check and state the result of each test (water, steam, acid) separately; zinc and iron are the standard examples where water says no and acid says yes.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating carbon or hydrogen as metals because they appear inside the same series list.
common_mistakes.why: Being listed in the same single sequence, in the same format as the named metals, makes them look like more entries of the same category.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that carbon and hydrogen are non-metal reference points before using the series, and never assign them a metallic property or a 'loses electrons to form Mn+' reaction.

exam_notes: When predicting a displacement reaction, always state both metals' series positions explicitly before giving the verdict; a correct final answer without this comparison may not gain full credit.
Always check a word or symbol equation for a displacement reaction is balanced atom by atom before giving it as a final answer.
When explaining displacement 'in terms of electrons', give both half-processes (the more reactive metal losing electrons, the less reactive metal's ion gaining them), not just one side.

summary.big_idea: The reactivity series is built from observed evidence (reactions with cold water, steam and dilute acid), and a more reactive metal, which loses electrons more readily, can displace a less reactive metal from its aqueous compound.
key_points: A metal's position in the series is read from which tests it reacts with: cold water (the most reactive metals only), steam (also magnesium, aluminium, zinc and iron) and dilute acid (every metal above hydrogen, with faster bubbling for more reactive metals).
The stated series: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, (carbon), zinc, iron, (hydrogen), copper, silver, gold.
Carbon and hydrogen are non-metal reference points, not metals, included for extraction and acid-reaction comparisons.
A displacement reaction occurs only when the added metal is more reactive than the metal already in the aqueous compound; the more reactive metal loses electrons to become the dissolved ion.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Before predicting any displacement, compare both metals' positions in the series: only the metal higher up (more reactive, loses electrons more readily) can displace the other.

exit_check.question: A metal M reacts with steam but not cold water, and reacts with dilute acid more vigorously than zinc but less vigorously than magnesium. Would M displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution?
exit_check.answer: Yes. M reacts with steam but not cold water, placing it in the magnesium-to-iron band; being more vigorous with acid than zinc means M is more reactive than zinc, so M would displace zinc from zinc sulfate solution.

epistemic_overrides.note: The reactivity series is a heuristic, not a fundamental law. The ordering can depend on reaction conditions (e.g., thermite reaction works despite aluminium being 'more reactive').
Metal extraction could include more industrial context and real-world connections.

04_Corrosion_and_protection.json.title: Corrosion and protection
04_Corrosion_and_protection.json.subject: Chemistry

objectives.statement: State the two conditions required for iron to rust and explain how painting, greasing or plastic-coating protect iron by acting as a physical barrier.

Explain galvanising as providing two separate protective mechanisms, a physical barrier and sacrificial oxidation of zinc, and explain why galvanised iron still resists rusting even where the zinc coating is scratched.

prerequisites.statement: A more reactive metal loses electrons more readily than a less reactive metal, and this ordering is fixed by the reactivity series.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Sacrificial protection in this lesson depends entirely on zinc being more reactive than iron, so it losing electrons preferentially is a direct application of the series, not a new separate fact.

prerequisites.statement: A controlled experiment changes only one variable at a time, so that the effect of that one variable on the outcome can be identified.
prerequisites.why_it_matters: Showing that rusting needs both oxygen and water, not just one of them, depends on comparing conditions that differ by only one variable at a time.

diagnostic_items.question: Write zinc, iron and tin in order of reactivity, most reactive first, and state which of the three loses electrons most readily.
diagnostic_items.expected_answer: Zinc, then iron, then tin. Zinc is the most reactive of the three, so zinc's atoms lose electrons most readily; tin is the least reactive, so tin's atoms lose electrons least readily.

common_wrong_answers.answer: Tin, iron, zinc, with tin losing electrons most readily.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner has the order reversed, or is ranking the metals by how familiar or 'precious' they seem rather than by their positions in the reactivity series.

common_wrong_answers.answer: All three are about equally reactive, because none of them reacts with cold water.
common_wrong_answers.interpretation: The learner treats a shared 'no reaction with cold water' result as meaning equal reactivity, missing that the series still orders metals finely within that group.

diagnostic_items.interpretation: Sacrificial protection in this lesson works only because zinc sits above iron and tin sits below it, and because 'more reactive' means 'loses electrons more readily'. A learner who cannot order these three, or who does not link the order to electron loss, will not be able to predict what happens at a scratch in a zinc coating as opposed to a tin one.
diagnostic_items.remediation_action: Ask the learner what would happen if each of the three metals in turn were placed in iron(II) sulfate solution; only the metal above iron, zinc, displaces the iron, which fixes the order from evidence rather than from memory.

theory_blocks.title: A nail that refuses to rust
theory_blocks.body:
Take two identical iron nails. Leave one on a windowsill in ordinary damp outdoor air for a week: it rusts.

Seal the second nail inside a container of water that has been boiled (to drive out dissolved gases) and then topped with a layer of oil so no more air can dissolve in: after the same week, this nail is still bright and unmarked.

Both nails had water nearby (damp air for one, liquid water for the other), so water alone cannot be the deciding factor; the nail that stayed shiny was specifically [[blue:the one kept away from oxygen as well]].

This comparison shows that water alone is not enough; a second test (a nail in dry air, with oxygen but no water, which also stays shiny) shows that oxygen alone is not enough either.

Together they give the rule that follows: rusting is not caused by water alone, nor by oxygen alone, but by the two together.

theory_blocks.title: Rust needs oxygen and water, both at once
theory_blocks.body:
**Rusting** is the corrosion of iron (and steel, which is mostly iron) into hydrated iron(III) oxide, a reddish-brown, flaky solid commonly just called rust. Rusting only happens when iron is in contact with **both** oxygen and water at the same time: $\text{iron} + \text{oxygen} + \text{water} \rightarrow \text{hydrated iron(III) oxide}$.

A controlled three-way comparison makes this precise, changing only one variable at a time: an iron nail kept in dry air (with a drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride, so no water is present) does not rust, because water is missing.

A nail kept in boiled, oxygen-free water sealed under oil does not rust either, because oxygen is missing. Only a nail with both water and dissolved oxygen available, such as one left in ordinary water open to the air, actually rusts.

assets.caption: Three identical iron nails under controlled conditions. Tube 1 is stoppered and the air inside is kept dry by anhydrous calcium chloride, so there is no water: no rust. Tube 2 is stoppered, the nail is completely covered by boiled water and a layer of oil floats on top, so no oxygen can reach it: no rust. Tube 3 is open to the air and the nail is covered by ordinary tap water, so both water and dissolved oxygen are present: it rusts.
assets.purpose: Makes the controlled comparison actually visible: only the third tube is open, only the second has an oil layer and only the first has a drying agent, so each tube is seen to be missing exactly one of the two requirements, or neither.

theory_blocks.title: A physical barrier keeps both requirements away
theory_blocks.body:
Because rusting needs both oxygen and water to reach the iron surface, one effective way to prevent it is to stop either (or both) from arriving there at all, by covering the iron with a continuous physical barrier.

**Painting**, **greasing/oiling** and **coating with plastic** all work this way: each forms an unbroken layer over the iron's surface that oxygen and water molecules simply cannot pass through. None of these methods changes the iron chemically or supplies it with anything; they succeed purely by exclusion, sealing the metal off from the two substances it needs to rust. The clear limitation of a barrier method is that it only works where the barrier itself is intact: a scratch, chip or crack in paint, grease or plastic coating exposes bare iron at exactly that point, and rusting can begin there even though the rest of the surface remains protected.

theory_blocks.title: Galvanising: a barrier plus a second, electrical mechanism
theory_blocks.body:
**Galvanising** coats steel with a layer of zinc, and it is easy to describe this as 'just another barrier coating', but galvanising actually protects iron in **two separate ways**, and treating them as one conflates two different mechanisms that behave very differently when the coating is damaged.

**Mechanism 1 (barrier):** the zinc layer physically covers the iron, keeping oxygen and water away, exactly like paint or grease.

**Mechanism 2 (sacrificial protection):** zinc is more reactive than iron, meaning zinc's atoms lose electrons more readily than iron's do. Where the coating is scratched and iron is exposed to oxygen and water, zinc still touching the iron continues to lose its electrons preferentially, $\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-$, and these electrons flow into the exposed iron, suppressing the iron's own tendency to lose electrons and rust. The zinc is said to be 'sacrificed': it slowly corrodes away in place of the iron, actively protecting the exposed metal rather than merely covering it.

The practical consequence of having two mechanisms is important: a scratched, galvanised nail resists rusting far longer than a scratched, painted nail, because the barrier failing at the scratch does not also end the sacrificial protection there;

a painted nail has no second mechanism to fall back on once its only barrier is broken.

assets.caption: Galvanised steel with a scratch exposing bare iron between two intact zinc-coated sections. Zinc, being more reactive, continues to lose electrons preferentially and these electrons flow into the exposed iron, protecting it even though the physical barrier is broken at the scratch.
assets.purpose: Makes the two separate mechanisms (barrier versus sacrificial) visible at the exact point, the scratch, where only one of them can still be working.

theory_blocks.title: A barrier metal is not automatically a sacrificial metal
theory_blocks.body:
The sacrificial mechanism specifically requires the coating metal to be [[blue:**more reactive**]] than the metal it is protecting.

Tin-plated steel (used for food cans) is the clear counter-example: tin is less reactive than iron, so a scratch in a tin coating does **not** give sacrificial protection;

the exposed iron rusts, and can rust even faster than uncoated iron, because iron is now the more reactive metal of the pair and loses electrons in preference to the tin.

'Coated with a metal' is therefore not, by itself, enough to guarantee sacrificial protection at a scratch: the coating metal's position in the reactivity series relative to iron has to be checked every time.

keywords.definition: The corrosion of iron into hydrated iron(III) oxide, which requires both oxygen and water to be present together.
Preventing corrosion by covering a metal's surface with a continuous physical layer (paint, grease, plastic) that keeps oxygen and water away.
Coating steel with zinc, which protects the iron both as a physical barrier and, where the barrier is broken, by sacrificial oxidation of the zinc.
Protection of a less reactive metal by a more reactive metal in contact with it, which loses its electrons preferentially and corrodes in the less reactive metal's place.
An experiment or comparison in which only one variable is changed at a time, so that its specific effect on the outcome can be identified.

worked_examples.statement: **Reading the controlled comparison.** State which of the three nail conditions (dry air; boiled water sealed under oil; ordinary water open to air) rusts, and explain why using only the two requirements for rusting.
solution: Dry air: no rust, because no water is present (one of the two requirements is missing, even though oxygen is present).
Boiled water sealed under oil: no rust, because no oxygen is present (the other requirement is missing, even though water is present).
Ordinary water open to air: rusts, because both water and dissolved oxygen are present together, satisfying both requirements at once.
worked_examples.interpretation: Walking through all three conditions explicitly, rather than only the one that rusts, rehearses the full controlled-comparison logic needed to counter the idea that water alone is enough to cause rusting.

worked_examples.statement: **Explaining a barrier failure.** A painted iron railing is chipped by a falling branch, exposing a small patch of bare iron. Explain what will happen at the chip over the following weeks, and why the rest of the railing remains unaffected.
solution: Paint protects iron purely by forming a physical barrier that keeps oxygen and water away from the metal surface; it has no second protective mechanism.
At the chip, bare iron is directly exposed to both oxygen and air moisture, satisfying both requirements for rusting, so rust will begin to form at that specific spot.
The rest of the railing, where the paint remains intact, still has its barrier working, keeping oxygen and water away from the iron underneath, so it stays protected and unaffected by the local chip.
worked_examples.interpretation: Localises the consequence of barrier failure to exactly the damaged area, preventing an over-generalisation that one chip ruins the whole railing's protection.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Assuming any single chip in a barrier coating means the entire object will now rust uniformly, rather than only at the exposed point.

worked_examples.statement: **Comparing two scratched coatings.** Two identical steel nails are scratched in the same way: nail P is galvanised (zinc-coated), nail Q is tin-plated. Predict which nail rusts faster at the scratch and explain the difference using reactivity.
solution: Both coatings lose their barrier function at the scratch, exposing bare iron to oxygen and water in both cases, so the barrier mechanism alone would predict no difference between P and Q.

Zinc (coating P) is more reactive than iron, so at the scratch, zinc continues to lose electrons preferentially, providing sacrificial protection to the exposed iron even though the barrier is broken there.
Tin (coating Q) is less reactive than iron, so it provides no sacrificial protection at its scratch; the exposed iron in nail Q is left to rust much as uncoated iron would.
Nail Q (tin-plated) rusts faster at the scratch than nail P (galvanised), because only nail P has a second, sacrificial mechanism still operating once the barrier has failed.
worked_examples.interpretation: Directly operationalises the earlier caveat about coating metals: the same type of coating failure (a scratch) produces very different outcomes depending purely on the coating metal's position in the reactivity series relative to iron.

guided_exercises.statement: Design a fourth test condition, different from the three already described (dry air; boiled water under oil; ordinary water open to air), that would provide further evidence for the two-requirement rule for rusting. State what result you would predict for your condition and why.
hints: The three existing conditions already cover 'oxygen but no water' (dry air), 'water but no oxygen' (boiled water under oil) and 'both' (ordinary water open to air); think about which combination is still missing, or how an existing condition could be made a stronger test.
A genuinely new test should still change only the relevant variables compared with an existing condition, keeping everything else the same.
State your prediction using the same two-requirement rule used for the other three conditions, not a new, separate idea.
guided_exercises.answer: One suitable fourth condition: an iron nail in a sealed tube of dry nitrogen (with a drying agent such as anhydrous calcium chloride), so that neither oxygen nor water is present. This is the one combination not among the original three. The predicted result is no rusting, because both requirements are missing, which confirms that nothing else in the set-up (the tube, the nail itself) causes rusting. Another valid answer is a nail sealed in dry, pure oxygen: a stronger version of the dry-air test, predicted not to rust because water is still missing, showing that even a high concentration of oxygen is not enough on its own.
common_errors: Proposing a condition that changes two variables at once (for example, warm salty water versus cold fresh water), which would not isolate the oxygen/water requirement cleanly.

guided_exercises.statement: A boat propeller shaft is made of steel. Engineers sometimes bolt a block of zinc, much larger than needed to coat the shaft, directly onto the shaft near the propeller, fully submerged in seawater, without covering the rest of the shaft in zinc at all. Explain why this still protects the steel shaft from rusting, using the sacrificial mechanism, and explain why the block, rather than a thin coating, is used here.
hints: The zinc block is not acting as a barrier at all here, since it does not cover the shaft's surface; think about which of the two galvanising mechanisms could still apply without any barrier.
Zinc and steel (mostly iron) are in direct electrical contact in seawater, which is itself a conducting liquid; connect this to the electron-flow description of sacrificial protection.
Think about why a large block, rather than a thin coating, might last longer in this specific, continuously immersed application.
guided_exercises.answer: The zinc block provides purely sacrificial protection, with no barrier role: because zinc is more reactive than iron and is bolted in direct electrical contact with the steel shaft, with the conducting seawater completing the circuit, zinc continues to lose its electrons preferentially ($\mathrm{Zn} \rightarrow \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} + 2e^-$), and these electrons flow through the shaft, suppressing the iron's own tendency to lose electrons and corrode, even though the zinc never physically covers the shaft's surface. A large block, rather than a thin coating, is used because the zinc itself slowly corrodes away as it does this job (it is genuinely 'sacrificed'), so a larger mass of zinc lasts much longer underwater before it is used up and needs replacing, compared with a thin coating that would be consumed quickly under continuous immersion.
common_errors: Describing the zinc block as a barrier covering the shaft, when the question explicitly states it does not cover the shaft's surface at all; only the sacrificial mechanism applies here.

exercises.statement: State the two conditions required for iron to rust, and name one everyday method of excluding each one from reaching an iron object.
exercises.answer: The two conditions required are the presence of oxygen and the presence of water, together. Both can be excluded from an iron object by the same method: covering it with an unbroken layer of paint, grease, oil or plastic, which forms a barrier that keeps both oxygen and water away from the metal surface at once.

exercises.statement: A student says: 'Galvanising is just painting with zinc instead of paint, so it works in exactly the same way.' Explain what is correct and what is incomplete about this statement.
exercises.answer: It is correct that galvanising does provide a barrier, exactly as paint does, keeping oxygen and water away from the iron surface while the zinc coating is intact. It is incomplete because galvanising also provides a second, different mechanism that paint does not have: sacrificial protection, in which zinc, being more reactive than iron, continues to lose electrons preferentially and protect exposed iron electrically even after the barrier itself is scratched or broken, something a simple paint barrier cannot do once damaged.

exercises.statement: Two identical uncoated iron nails are placed in sealed jars: jar A contains only nitrogen gas and water that has been boiled to remove dissolved oxygen; jar B contains ordinary air and the same boiled water. Predict which jar's nail rusts, with a reason, and state what this comparison specifically demonstrates.
exercises.answer: The nail in jar B rusts; the nail in jar A does not. Jar A supplies water but not oxygen (nitrogen gas contains no oxygen, and boiling removed the oxygen dissolved in the water), so one of the two requirements for rusting is missing; jar B supplies both water and the oxygen present in ordinary air (which dissolves into the water), satisfying both requirements. This comparison specifically demonstrates that oxygen, not just any gas or atmosphere, is the required second ingredient alongside water, since replacing air with an oxygen-free gas (nitrogen) is enough to stop rusting even with water still present.
common_errors: Concluding that jar A's nail does not rust simply because it is sealed, rather than correctly identifying that the absence of oxygen specifically, not sealing itself, is the reason.

exercises.statement: A new alloy coating for steel bridges is proposed, made from a metal less reactive than iron but highly resistant to corrosion itself. Using the two galvanising mechanisms as a model, predict what would happen if this coating were scratched, and explain why this coating would behave differently from a zinc (galvanised) coating at the scratch.
exercises.answer: If this new coating were scratched, only the barrier mechanism would have been providing protection, since the coating metal is less reactive than iron and so cannot provide sacrificial protection; iron is more reactive than this coating metal, which means at the scratch, the exposed iron would continue to lose its own electrons and corrode, with the less reactive coating metal doing nothing to prevent this (and, by the same reactivity argument used for tin-plated steel, potentially making the local corrosion slightly worse rather than better). This differs from a zinc coating specifically because zinc is more reactive than iron: at a scratch, zinc continues to lose electrons preferentially and protects the exposed iron electrically, a mechanism this new, less-reactive coating could never provide, however corrosion-resistant the coating metal is in its own right.

exam_questions.statement: Explain why an iron nail kept in a sealed jar of dry oxygen gas does not rust, and why an iron nail kept in boiled water sealed under a layer of oil also does not rust, even though these two set-ups seem very different.
exam_questions.answer: Rusting requires both oxygen and water to be present together; each of these two set-ups supplies only one of the two requirements. The nail in dry oxygen gas has oxygen available but no water (the gas and the jar are kept dry), so it does not rust. The nail in boiled water sealed under oil has water available, but the boiling removes dissolved oxygen from the water and the oil layer prevents further oxygen from the air dissolving back in, so no oxygen is available either, and it does not rust. Although the two set-ups look different, they are equivalent in the one way that matters: each is missing exactly one of the two substances iron needs to rust.
mark_scheme: States that rusting requires both oxygen and water together.
Explains that the dry-oxygen jar is missing water.
Explains that the boiled/oiled water is missing (dissolved) oxygen.
Explicitly connects both cases to the same underlying two-requirement rule, rather than treating them as two unrelated explanations.

exam_questions.statement: A steel ship's hull is protected in two ways: it is painted, and zinc blocks are bolted to the hull below the waterline. Explain the separate purpose of each method, and explain what would happen to the protection at a point where the paint is scratched but no zinc block is nearby.
exam_questions.answer: The paint provides a physical barrier over most of the hull's surface, keeping oxygen and water away from the steel wherever the paint remains intact; it protects the large area of the hull that cannot practically be covered in zinc blocks. The zinc blocks provide sacrificial protection: because zinc is more reactive than iron, it loses electrons preferentially, and this effect can extend some distance along the electrically connected steel hull through the seawater, suppressing the iron's tendency to corrode even in areas not directly coated with zinc. At a point where the paint is scratched and no zinc block is nearby, the barrier mechanism has failed locally, and if the sacrificial effect from the distant zinc blocks is too weak to reach that specific point effectively, the exposed steel at the scratch is at risk of rusting, since neither mechanism is working strongly there.
mark_scheme: States that paint acts as a physical barrier, protecting most of the hull's surface.
States that the zinc blocks provide sacrificial protection because zinc is more reactive than iron.
Explains that sacrificial protection can act at a distance through the electrically connected, seawater-immersed hull.
Explains that a scratch far from any zinc block is at risk because both mechanisms are weak or absent there.
States that zinc loses electrons / is oxidised (corrodes) in preference to the iron of the hull.

challenge_questions.statement:
**Six test tubes.** Six identical iron nails are set up as shown and left for two weeks.

| Tube | Set-up |
|---|---|
| 1 | nail covered by tap water, tube open to the air |
| 2 | nail completely covered by boiled water with a layer of oil on top, tube stoppered |
| 3 | nail in dry air over anhydrous calcium chloride, tube stoppered |
| 4 | nail tightly wrapped in magnesium ribbon, covered by tap water, tube open to the air |
| 5 | nail tightly wrapped in copper wire, covered by tap water, tube open to the air |
| 6 | nail completely coated in grease, covered by tap water, tube open to the air |

(a) State which nails rust and which do not, giving a reason for each tube that does not rust.
(b) One nail rusts noticeably **more** than the nail in tube 1. Identify it and explain why.
(c) Tubes 4 and 6 both keep their nail bright, but by different mechanisms. Name each mechanism, and state which of the two would still protect the nail if the magnesium or the grease were scratched through in one small place.
hints: Check each tube against the two requirements for rusting first; only then ask whether a protection mechanism is at work.
For (b), compare copper's reactivity with iron's, and recall what the lesson says about a scratch in tin-plated steel.
For (c), one of the two mechanisms works only while a covering is unbroken; the other depends on reactivity and keeps working at a break.
challenge_questions.answer:
(a) The nails in tubes 1 and 5 rust. The nails in tubes 2, 3, 4 and 6 do not. Tube 2 has water but no oxygen, because boiling drove the dissolved oxygen out and the oil layer stops more air dissolving in. Tube 3 has oxygen but no water, because the anhydrous calcium chloride keeps the air dry. Tubes 4 and 6 have both requirements present, so the nail is kept bright by protection rather than by a missing requirement: magnesium protects the nail in tube 4 and the grease protects it in tube 6.

(b) The nail in tube 5. Copper is less reactive than iron, so where the two metals are in contact in water it is the **iron** that loses electrons preferentially; the iron is oxidised in place of the copper and rusts faster than the unwrapped nail in tube 1. This is the same reasoning that applies to a scratch in tin-plated steel.

(c) Tube 4 is sacrificial protection: magnesium is more reactive than iron, so magnesium loses electrons, $\mathrm{Mg} \rightarrow \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} + 2e^-$, in preference to the iron. Tube 6 is barrier protection: the grease simply keeps oxygen and water away from the iron surface. Only tube 4's protection survives a small scratch, because the magnesium still touching the nail goes on losing electrons preferentially and protects the exposed iron; a scratch through the grease exposes bare iron to both oxygen and water, with no second mechanism to fall back on.
common_errors: Predicting that tube 5 behaves like tube 4, on the assumption that wrapping a nail in any metal protects it.
Saying the nail in tube 2 is safe 'because the tube is sealed', rather than because the boiled water and the oil layer leave no oxygen available.

mcq.stem: Which pair of conditions, both present together, causes iron to rust?

options.text: Water alone, regardless of oxygen
options.why_wrong: iron kept in oxygen-free water (for example, boiled and sealed under oil) does not rust, showing water alone is not sufficient.

options.text: Oxygen alone, regardless of water
options.why_wrong: iron kept in dry oxygen gas does not rust, showing oxygen alone is not sufficient.

options.text: Oxygen and water
Heat and pressure, with no requirement for oxygen or water
options.why_wrong: rusting is not caused by heat or pressure in this way; the controlled comparisons specifically isolate oxygen and water as the two requirements.

mcq.explanation: Controlled comparisons show that iron rusts only when both oxygen and water are present together; removing either one alone stops rusting.

mcq.stem: How does a coating of grease protect an iron tool from rusting?

options.text: By supplying a controlled, slow release of oxygen to the iron
options.why_wrong: grease does not supply oxygen at all; its role is to keep oxygen and water away from the surface entirely.

options.text: By reacting chemically with the iron to form a more resistant alloy
options.why_wrong: grease does not react chemically with the iron at all; it works by physical exclusion, not by changing the iron's composition.

options.text: By being more reactive than iron and corroding sacrificially in its place
options.why_wrong: grease is not a metal and has no reactivity to compare against iron's; this sacrificial mechanism applies to zinc in galvanising, not to grease.

options.text: By forming a physical barrier that keeps oxygen and water away from the iron surface

mcq.explanation: Grease, like paint and plastic coatings, protects purely by forming a continuous physical barrier that keeps oxygen and water away from the iron surface underneath.

mcq.stem: A galvanised iron sheet is deeply scratched, exposing bare iron. Which statement correctly describes what happens at the scratch?

options.text: The nearby zinc continues to lose electrons preferentially, protecting the exposed iron even though the barrier is broken there
The exposed iron rusts immediately and at the same rate as unprotected bare iron, since the zinc coating no longer covers that point
options.why_wrong: this treats galvanising as having only the barrier mechanism; zinc still provides sacrificial protection at the scratch because it is more reactive than iron.

options.text: The scratch has no effect at all, because zinc coatings cannot be physically damaged
options.why_wrong: zinc coatings can certainly be scratched or chipped; the question specifically describes this happening.

options.text: The iron is now protected only because the scratch exposes a larger surface area of zinc elsewhere
options.why_wrong: the protection at the scratch comes from zinc's reactivity relative to iron (sacrificial protection), not from the total surface area of zinc elsewhere on the sheet.

mcq.explanation: Because zinc is more reactive than iron, it continues to lose electrons preferentially at the scratch, providing sacrificial protection even though the physical barrier has failed there.

mcq.stem: A steel food can is coated with tin on the inside. If this coating is scratched, what would you predict about sacrificial protection at the scratch, and why?

options.text: Tin would sacrificially protect the exposed iron, because tin is more reactive than iron
options.why_wrong: tin is actually less reactive than iron, not more, so this reasoning and its conclusion are both incorrect.

options.text: No sacrificial protection would occur, because tin is less reactive than iron
Sacrificial protection would occur regardless of reactivity, because any metal coating protects any other metal this way
options.why_wrong: sacrificial protection specifically requires the coating metal to be more reactive than the protected metal; it is not a general property of 'any metal coating'.

options.text: The scratch would have no effect, because tin coatings cannot corrode
options.why_wrong: tin, like other metals, can corrode; the question is specifically about whether it protects the exposed iron sacrificially, which depends on relative reactivity.

mcq.explanation: Tin is less reactive than iron, so unlike zinc, it cannot provide sacrificial protection at a scratch; only the barrier mechanism was ever available from a tin coating.

flashcards.front: What two conditions, together, are required for iron to rust?
flashcards.back: Oxygen and water, both present at the same time.

flashcards.front: How does a paint coating protect iron from rusting?
flashcards.back: By forming a continuous physical barrier that keeps both oxygen and water away from the iron surface; it does not react with or supply anything to the iron.

flashcards.front: What is the key difference between how paint and galvanising protect iron?
flashcards.back: Paint provides only a physical barrier; galvanising provides a physical barrier plus sacrificial protection, because zinc is more reactive than iron and keeps protecting exposed iron even where the barrier is scratched.

flashcards.front: If a galvanised nail is scratched, does the exposed iron rust immediately, just like bare iron would?
flashcards.back: No. The nearby zinc, being more reactive than iron, continues to lose electrons preferentially, protecting the exposed iron sacrificially even though the barrier is broken at the scratch.

flashcards.front: A scratched tin-plated steel can shows rusting at the scratch, but a scratched galvanised iron sheet does not rust at its scratch for a long time. Why the difference?
flashcards.back: Tin is less reactive than iron, so it gives no sacrificial protection at a scratch; zinc is more reactive than iron, so it does, protecting the exposed iron even after the barrier fails.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Water alone is enough to make iron rust, with oxygen playing no essential role.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Iron left in or near water is the most familiar everyday image of rusting, so water looks like the whole cause, and the oxygen dissolved in or available to that water is invisible and easy to overlook.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that iron in boiled, oxygen-free water (with no air contact) will rust just as readily as iron in ordinary open water.
misconceptions.correct_model: Rusting needs both oxygen and water present together; iron kept in water with the dissolved oxygen removed (and no further air contact) does not rust, which is exactly why a layer of oil floated on boiled water is used to keep a nail rust-free in a controlled experiment.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare, side by side, iron in ordinary tap water (open to air) with iron in boiled water sealed under a layer of oil, and ask what single variable differs between the two set-ups.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: A protective coating such as paint works by supplying oxygen to the iron in a controlled way, rather than by keeping oxygen out.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Learners sometimes assume any coating that 'does something chemical-sounding' to a reactive metal must be adding a reactive substance, rather than considering that its role might be to block access entirely.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes paint as 'giving' or 'controlling' oxygen reaching the iron, instead of describing it as sealing the surface so that neither oxygen nor water can reach the metal at all.
misconceptions.correct_model: Paint, grease and plastic coatings protect iron by forming a continuous physical barrier that keeps both oxygen and water away from the metal surface entirely; they do not supply, release or control any oxygen themselves, and protection fails specifically at any point where the barrier is broken or scratched.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask directly what paint is made of and whether it could plausibly be a source of oxygen, then redirect to 'what does the barrier keep out, not what does it let in or supply'.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Zinc protects galvanised iron only while the zinc coating is physically unbroken; once scratched, the iron underneath is left just as unprotected as bare iron.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: The barrier mechanism (which does fail once broken) is the first and more intuitive idea learners meet, so it gets applied automatically to galvanising as well, without separately considering zinc's own reactivity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner predicts that a scratched galvanised nail will rust exactly as fast as an identical scratched, uncoated iron nail.
misconceptions.correct_model: Galvanising provides two separate mechanisms: a physical barrier (which does fail at a scratch, exactly like paint) and sacrificial protection, in which the zinc, being more reactive than iron, loses its electrons preferentially and continues to protect the exposed iron electrically even after the barrier itself is broken at that scratch.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a scratched painted nail (which rusts at the scratch, since paint has only the barrier mechanism) with a scratched galvanised nail (which resists rusting at the scratch for a considerable time, since zinc still protects it sacrificially), making the two-mechanism difference an observed contrast, not an assertion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Explaining rusting using only water, or only oxygen, as if either alone were sufficient.
common_mistakes.why: Water is the more visually obvious ingredient in everyday rusting, so the equally necessary role of dissolved oxygen is easy to leave out.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always state both requirements together and name a controlled comparison (dry air; oxygen-free water) that shows each one is independently necessary.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing a barrier coating (paint, grease, plastic) as supplying or controlling oxygen, rather than excluding both oxygen and water.
common_mistakes.why: Any protective coating applied to a reactive metal can sound like it is 'doing something chemical' to the metal, rather than simply blocking access to it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: State explicitly that a barrier coating works by exclusion: it keeps oxygen and water away from the surface, and does not react with, or supply anything to, the iron underneath.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating galvanising as having only a barrier mechanism, predicting that a scratch removes all protection immediately.
common_mistakes.why: The barrier mechanism is simpler and is met first, so it is easy to apply it to galvanising without separately considering zinc's reactivity.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always name both galvanising mechanisms (barrier and sacrificial) separately, and check specifically what happens to each one at a scratch, rather than describing galvanising as a single mechanism.

exam_notes: Always state rusting's two requirements (oxygen and water) together, as a pair, and never describe either one as sufficient on its own.
When explaining a barrier coating, state clearly that it works by exclusion (keeping substances away), not by supplying or chemically changing anything.
For galvanising questions, always separate the two mechanisms explicitly and state what happens to each one at a scratch; marks are commonly allocated to each mechanism separately.

summary.big_idea: Rusting needs both oxygen and water together; a barrier coating protects by excluding both, while galvanising adds a second mechanism, sacrificial protection by zinc, that keeps working even where the barrier itself is broken.
key_points: Rusting of iron requires both oxygen and water present at the same time; removing either one alone stops rusting.
Paint, grease and plastic coatings protect by forming a physical barrier that excludes both oxygen and water; this protection fails specifically wherever the barrier is broken.

Galvanising provides two separate mechanisms: a physical barrier, and sacrificial protection, in which zinc, being more reactive than iron, loses electrons preferentially and protects exposed iron even at a scratch.

Sacrificial protection requires the coating metal to be more reactive than the protected metal; tin-plated steel, where tin is less reactive than iron, has no sacrificial mechanism and only ever had a barrier.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Rusting needs oxygen and water together; a barrier keeps both out but fails at damage, while galvanising's zinc also protects a scratch sacrificially because zinc is more reactive than iron.

exit_check.question: A steel garden gate is coated with a metal less reactive than iron, purely as a decorative, shiny finish. If this coating is scratched, would you expect the same long-lasting protection at the scratch as a galvanised (zinc-coated) gate would show? Explain.
exit_check.answer: No. Because the decorative coating metal is less reactive than iron, it cannot provide sacrificial protection; only the barrier mechanism was ever present, so a scratch exposes the iron with no second mechanism to fall back on, unlike a galvanised gate, where the more reactive zinc continues to protect the exposed iron at the scratch.

epistemic_overrides.note: The reactivity series is a heuristic, not a fundamental law. The ordering can depend on reaction conditions (e.g., thermite reaction works despite aluminium being 'more reactive').
