theory_blocks.title: Why gold needs no chemistry, and aluminium needs a lot
theory_blocks.body:
Gold has been mined and used for thousands of years, often found as small, pure nuggets or flakes that need no chemical processing at all beyond physically separating them from surrounding rock.

Aluminium, despite being far more abundant in the Earth's crust than gold, was not produced cheaply and in bulk until the late nineteenth century,

and it needed an entire new industrial process (electrolysis, powered by large amounts of electricity) to achieve it.

[[blue:The difference is not abundance; it is reactivity.]] Gold is so unreactive that it stays as the pure metal in the ground, needing no chemical extraction step at all. Aluminium is so reactive that it is never found uncombined, and its compounds are held together so strongly that no ordinary chemical reducing agent available in large, cheap quantities (such as carbon) can pull the oxygen away from it; only the much more forceful intervention of electrolysis can. A metal's position in the reactivity series, not how common it is, decides how hard it is to extract.

theory_blocks.title: Reading the extraction method from the series
theory_blocks.body:
The reactivity series, already built from water/steam/acid evidence, also predicts the method needed to extract a metal from its naturally occurring compound (its ore):

- **Metals more reactive than carbon** (potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium): their compounds are too chemically stable for carbon to reduce; these metals are extracted by **electrolysis** of a molten compound.
- **Metals less reactive than carbon but more reactive than hydrogen** (zinc, iron) and some below hydrogen (copper, to a useful extent): carbon (as carbon or carbon monoxide) is reactive enough to remove the oxygen from these metals' oxides; these metals are extracted by **reduction with carbon** or carbon monoxide.
- **The least reactive metals** (silver, gold): these barely react with anything in the ground, so they are commonly **found native**, as the uncombined element, needing no chemical extraction step at all, only physical separation from surrounding rock.

The general principle behind the carbon/electrolysis boundary: a less reactive element cannot remove oxygen from a compound of a more reactive element, because the more reactive element holds onto its bond to oxygen more strongly;

carbon being below aluminium (but above zinc and iron) in the series is exactly why it works for iron's ore but not for aluminium's.

assets.caption: Extraction method read directly from reactivity: metals more reactive than carbon (potassium to aluminium) require electrolysis; metals below carbon (zinc, iron, copper) are extracted by reduction with carbon/carbon monoxide; the least reactive metals (silver, gold) are commonly found native.
assets.purpose: Converts 'which method for which metal' from a list to be memorised into a single readable consequence of the one series already built in lesson 3.

theory_blocks.title: Iron: reduction of iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace
theory_blocks.body:
Iron's main ore is **hematite**, which contains iron(III) oxide, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$. Because iron sits **below carbon** in the reactivity series, carbon is reactive enough to take the oxygen away from it,

so iron does not need the much more expensive route of electrolysis.

The statement to know is this: [[blue:iron from hematite is extracted by reduction of iron(III) oxide in the blast furnace]].

'Reduction' here carries its usual meaning of **loss of oxygen**: the $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ loses its oxygen and molten iron is left, which runs to the bottom of the furnace and is tapped off.

The individual reactions inside the furnace that bring this about are set out in the next block, which is tagged ADVANCED.

theory_blocks.title: Why carbon cannot do aluminium's job
theory_blocks.body:
It is tempting to assume carbon reduction could work for any metal oxide, with a hot enough furnace making up the difference; it cannot.

[[blue:Aluminium is more reactive than carbon]], which means aluminium's bond to oxygen in aluminium oxide is stronger than any bond carbon could offer to replace it with;

no amount of extra heat changes which element is more reactive. Aluminium is therefore extracted from purified aluminium oxide (obtained from the ore bauxite) by **electrolysis** of the molten compound instead, using a large electrical current to force the reduction that carbon chemically cannot provide.

Electrolysis is a far more energy-intensive process than carbon reduction, which is the direct, practical reason aluminium historically cost far more to produce than iron, despite being more abundant in the Earth's crust.

theory_blocks.title: The blast-furnace reactions in sequence
theory_blocks.body:
**Extension beyond Core (Supplement C9.6.4).** Three reactions, in sequence, carry out the reduction inside the furnace.

**1. The coke burns.** Coke (nearly pure carbon) burns in the blast of hot air. This provides the heat the furnace needs and produces carbon dioxide:

$\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}}$

**2. The carbon dioxide is reduced to carbon monoxide.** Higher up the furnace, this carbon dioxide meets more hot coke:

$\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{CO_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}$ (checked: C 2 and O 2 on each side)

**3. The carbon monoxide reduces the iron(III) oxide.** It is the carbon monoxide, not the solid carbon, that removes the oxygen from the ore:

$\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + 3\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ (checked: Fe 2, O 6 and C 3 on each side)

In that third reaction the iron(III) oxide is **reduced**, because it loses oxygen, and the carbon monoxide is **oxidised**, because it gains oxygen; the two changes are two descriptions of the same single reaction, not two separate steps.

theory_blocks.title: Limestone's separate job: removing impurities as slag
theory_blocks.body:
Limestone ($\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$) is added to the blast furnace alongside the iron ore, but it contains no iron at all and takes no part in reducing the ore; its job is entirely separate.

Heat decomposes it: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$. The calcium oxide formed then reacts with silica ($\mathrm{SiO_{2}}$), a sandy impurity present in the iron ore, forming molten calcium silicate: $\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{SiO_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$ (checked: Ca 1, Si 1, O 3 on each side).

This calcium silicate is the **slag**: being less dense than molten iron, it floats on top of the iron inside the furnace and is tapped off separately,

carrying the unwanted impurities away from the iron and leaving the tapped iron considerably purer than the original ore.

assets.caption: Vertical section through the blast furnace: the charge (hematite, coke, limestone) goes in at the top and waste gases leave at the top, while the hot air blast enters near the base. At the bottom the two liquids settle into separate layers — denser molten iron at the very bottom, run off through the lowest taphole, with the less dense molten slag ($\mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$) floating on top of it and tapped through a clearly higher hole.
assets.purpose: Shows the furnace as a flow of named inputs to named, chemically distinct outputs, blocking the limestone-as-iron-source and slag-as-impure-iron misconceptions by making every input and output a separately labelled formula.

keywords.definition: Iron(III) oxide, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$, the main ore from which iron is extracted.
The ore from which aluminium oxide is obtained, before aluminium is extracted from it by electrolysis.
The industrial furnace in which iron ore is reduced to molten iron using carbon monoxide generated from coke and a hot air blast.
Molten calcium silicate, $\mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$, formed from limestone's calcium oxide reacting with silica impurities in the ore; floats on molten iron and is tapped off separately.
Occurring naturally as the pure, uncombined element, typical of the least reactive metals such as gold and silver.

worked_examples.statement: **Choosing a method from the series.** State, with a reason, which extraction method (electrolysis or carbon reduction) would be appropriate for a metal found just below zinc in the reactivity series.
solution: A metal just below zinc is also below carbon in the series (since zinc itself sits below carbon).
Carbon reduction is appropriate for metals below carbon in the series, because carbon is reactive enough to remove oxygen from their oxides.
This metal should therefore be extracted by reduction with carbon (or carbon monoxide), not by electrolysis.
worked_examples.interpretation: Rehearses the single rule (compare position to carbon, not to any specific named metal) on a position described only relatively, preparing for an unfamiliar-metal question.

worked_examples.statement: **Balancing and reading the reduction step.** Confirm that $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + 3\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_{2}}$ is balanced, and state what is being reduced and what is being oxidised.
solution: Left side atom count: Fe = 2 and O = 3 (in Fe2O3), plus C = 3 and O = 3 (in 3CO), so O = 6 in total. Right side: Fe = 2 (in 2Fe), plus C = 3 and O = 6 (in 3CO2). Both sides match: Fe 2, O 6, C 3; the equation is balanced.
Iron(III) oxide is reduced: it loses oxygen, going from $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ to $\mathrm{Fe}$.
Carbon monoxide is oxidised: it gains oxygen, going from $\mathrm{CO}$ to $\mathrm{CO_{2}}$.
worked_examples.interpretation: Separating the balance check from the reduced/oxidised identification reinforces that 'reduction' here means oxygen loss specifically, reusing the Prerequisite definition rather than introducing a new one.
worked_examples.common_mistake: Stating that iron is 'produced' without identifying the reduction explicitly as oxygen loss from Fe2O3.

worked_examples.statement: **Tracing limestone's role.** A student claims that without limestone, the blast furnace would simply produce less iron. Evaluate this claim and state what would actually happen to the iron produced if limestone were left out.
solution: Limestone contains no iron and plays no part in the reduction reaction that actually produces iron from hematite; removing it would not reduce the quantity of iron(III) oxide being reduced, so the claim that 'less iron' would be produced is not correct for this reason.
Limestone's actual role is removing silica impurities from the ore, by decomposing to calcium oxide and then reacting with silica to form slag.

Without limestone, these silica impurities would have nowhere to go: they would remain mixed in with the molten iron, producing a lower-purity (more contaminated) iron, rather than a smaller quantity of pure iron.
worked_examples.interpretation: The result follows from the scientific principle used in the solution and shows how to apply that principle when the context or data change.

guided_exercises.statement: An unfamiliar metal, Q, is found to sit between aluminium and carbon in the reactivity series. State, with a reason, which extraction method would be appropriate for metal Q, and explain why this question can be answered without knowing anything else about Q.
hints: Locate the one boundary that actually decides the method: a metal's position relative to carbon, not its exact identity.
Metal Q sits above carbon (since it is between aluminium and carbon, and aluminium is above carbon).
State the method that applies to every metal above carbon in the series, regardless of which specific metal it is.
guided_exercises.answer: Metal Q should be extracted by electrolysis. Because Q sits above carbon in the series (between aluminium and carbon), carbon is not reactive enough to reduce Q's oxide, exactly as it cannot reduce aluminium oxide; this question can be answered without knowing Q's exact identity because the extraction method depends only on a metal's position relative to carbon, not on any other specific property of that metal.
common_errors: Refusing to answer because 'metal Q is not a real, named metal', missing that the method rule is general and does not require knowing the metal's identity.

guided_exercises.statement: Put these four blast-furnace events in the correct order, and state the equation for each: coke burns in the hot air blast; iron(III) oxide is reduced; limestone decomposes; calcium oxide reacts with silica to form slag.
hints: Coke burning needs only the incoming hot air blast and is not waiting on any other named step, so think about which event could happen first.
The carbon monoxide needed to reduce the iron ore has to exist before the reduction step can happen; where does carbon monoxide actually come from?
Calcium oxide has to exist before it can react with silica, so limestone's decomposition must come before the final slag-forming step.
guided_exercises.answer: Order: (1) Coke burns in the hot air blast, $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}}$, and further coke reacts with this to form carbon monoxide, $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{CO_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}$. (2) Iron(III) oxide is reduced by this carbon monoxide, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + 3\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_{2}}$. (3) Limestone decomposes in the furnace's heat, $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$. (4) The calcium oxide formed reacts with silica impurities to form slag, $\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{SiO_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$. (Steps 1-2 and steps 3-4 each happen continuously and can overlap in time inside the furnace; the dependency that matters is that carbon monoxide must exist before step 2, and calcium oxide must exist before step 4.)
common_errors: Placing the slag-forming reaction before limestone's decomposition, missing that calcium oxide (needed for the slag reaction) is itself a product of that decomposition.

exercises.statement: State the main ore of iron and the main ore of aluminium, by name and formula where given, and state the extraction method used for each.
exercises.answer: Iron's main ore is hematite, iron(III) oxide, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$, extracted by reduction with carbon monoxide in a blast furnace. Aluminium's main ore is bauxite, from which purified aluminium oxide is obtained; aluminium is extracted from this purified oxide by electrolysis.

exercises.statement: Explain why aluminium cannot be extracted from aluminium oxide using carbon, however hot the furnace is made.
exercises.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so aluminium's bond to oxygen in aluminium oxide is stronger than any bond carbon could form in its place; carbon simply is not reactive enough to remove this oxygen, and this relative-reactivity relationship does not change with temperature, so no amount of extra heat allows carbon to do the job instead.

exercises.statement: Balance and check this equation for limestone's decomposition, and state the name of each product: $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$.
exercises.answer: Checking atoms: left side Ca 1, C 1, O 3; right side Ca 1 (in CaO) + 0, O 1 (in CaO) + 2 (in CO2) = 3, C 1 (in CO2); both sides have Ca 1, C 1, O 3, so the equation is already balanced as written, with no coefficients needed. The products are calcium oxide ($\mathrm{CaO}$) and carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_{2}}$).
common_errors: Assuming every furnace equation must need large coefficients, and adding unnecessary numbers to an equation that is already balanced 1:1:1.

exercises.statement: Titanium is a metal more reactive than carbon but less reactive than aluminium, and in practice it is extracted by a specialised chemical process rather than by the ordinary electrolysis used for aluminium, partly because titanium's electrolysis route is unusually difficult to run economically. Using only the general reactivity rule from this lesson, state what the rule alone would predict about whether carbon reduction could work for titanium, and explain why the rule does not, by itself, guarantee that electrolysis will always be the economically easiest method just because it is the chemically required one.
exercises.answer: Because titanium is more reactive than carbon, the general rule predicts that carbon cannot reduce titanium's oxide, in exactly the same way it cannot reduce aluminium oxide; titanium therefore needs a method that does not rely on carbon as the reducing agent: either electrolysis or, as is done in practice, reduction by a metal that is more reactive than titanium (such as magnesium). The rule only predicts which methods are chemically ruled out (carbon reduction, in this case) based on relative reactivity; it says nothing about which of the remaining, chemically possible methods will turn out to be the cheapest or most practical to run at an industrial scale, which is a separate, economic and engineering question that the reactivity series alone cannot answer.

exam_questions.statement: Explain, using the reactivity series, why iron can be extracted from its ore using carbon, while aluminium cannot, and name the method actually used for aluminium instead.
exam_questions.answer: Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon (as carbon monoxide, inside a blast furnace) is reactive enough to remove the oxygen from iron(III) oxide, reducing it to iron metal. Aluminium, in contrast, is more reactive than carbon, so aluminium's bond to oxygen in aluminium oxide is stronger than any bond carbon could offer instead; carbon cannot remove this oxygen, at any practical furnace temperature, because the relative reactivity relationship between aluminium and carbon does not change with temperature. Aluminium is instead extracted by electrolysis of molten (purified) aluminium oxide, using an electric current to force the reduction that carbon chemically cannot provide.
mark_scheme: States that iron is less reactive than carbon.
States that carbon (as carbon monoxide) can reduce iron(III) oxide as a result.
States that aluminium is more reactive than carbon.
Explains that carbon therefore cannot reduce aluminium oxide, and that heat does not change this.
Names electrolysis as the method actually used for aluminium.

exam_questions.statement: A blast furnace is charged with hematite, coke, limestone and a blast of hot air. Trace the sequence of reactions that leads to (a) the production of molten iron, and (b) the production of slag, giving a balanced equation for each key step you describe.
exam_questions.answer: (a) Coke burns in the hot air blast, $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{2}}$; further coke reacts with this carbon dioxide to form carbon monoxide, $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{CO_{2}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{CO}$; this carbon monoxide then reduces the iron(III) oxide in the hematite, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}} + 3\mathrm{CO} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe} + 3\mathrm{CO_{2}}$, producing molten iron, which is tapped from the bottom of the furnace. (b) Limestone decomposes in the furnace's heat, $\mathrm{CaCO_{3}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_{2}}$; the calcium oxide produced reacts with silica impurities present in the ore, $\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{SiO_{2}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$, forming molten calcium silicate (slag), which floats on the denser molten iron and is tapped off separately.
mark_scheme: Gives the balanced equation for coke combustion, C + O2 -> CO2.
Gives the balanced equation for carbon monoxide formation, C + CO2 -> 2CO.
Gives the balanced equation for iron(III) oxide reduction, Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, and links it to molten iron.
Gives the balanced equation for limestone decomposition, CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2.
Gives the balanced equation for slag formation, CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3.
Correctly separates the two output streams (molten iron tapped from the bottom; slag floating above and tapped separately).

challenge_questions.statement: A geologist finds a metal, R, as small uncombined nuggets in a riverbed, never as a compound in the surrounding rock. A chemist separately measures that R does not react with cold water, steam, or dilute acid, even after a long time. Using both pieces of evidence together, and the general reasoning used for carbon versus aluminium, justify where in the reactivity series R most likely belongs, and explain whether electrolysis would ever be a sensible industrial method for obtaining R.
hints: Being found uncombined in nature is itself evidence about reactivity; connect this directly to the 'found native' band of the extraction ladder.
The separate chemical test (no reaction with water, steam or acid) should be checked for consistency with the 'found native' conclusion, not treated as a second, unrelated fact.
Electrolysis is used specifically to force a reduction that is otherwise too difficult chemically; think about whether that difficulty applies to a metal that barely reacts with anything at all.
challenge_questions.answer: Both pieces of evidence point to the same conclusion: metal R is among the least reactive metals, similar in position to silver or gold. Being found as uncombined nuggets means R's compounds, if they ever formed naturally, are so unstable (or R simply never reacted with anything available in the rock) that the pure element survives in the ground; this is exactly the 'found native' pattern used for the least reactive metals. The chemical test is fully consistent with this: a metal unreactive enough to never react with water, steam or dilute acid is unreactive enough that it would not have formed stable compounds in the rock in the first place, matching the geological observation rather than contradicting it. Electrolysis would not be a sensible method for R: electrolysis is needed specifically to force the reduction of very stable compounds of highly reactive metals (such as aluminium oxide), and R, being found already as the pure element, needs no chemical extraction step at all, only physical separation from the surrounding rock or sediment; using electrolysis here would be solving a reduction problem that does not exist for R.
challenge_questions.full_solution: Evidence 1 (geological): found uncombined -> matches the found-native band (least reactive metals, e.g. silver, gold), since these metals' compounds, where they can even form, are unstable enough, or reactions rare enough, that the pure element persists naturally. Evidence 2 (chemical): no reaction with water/steam/acid -> independently places R among the least reactive metals in the series, the same band identified from evidence 1. Consistency check: both pieces of evidence agree, with no contradiction, so the combined conclusion (R belongs with the least reactive metals) is well supported, not merely assumed from one piece of evidence alone. Electrolysis judgement: electrolysis exists to force reduction of compounds too stable for carbon to reduce (true for highly reactive metals like aluminium); R, being this unreactive, forms no such stable compound needing to be reduced at all, so electrolysis addresses a problem R does not have, and is not a sensible method for it.
common_errors: Treating the geological observation and the chemical test as two separate, unconnected facts rather than checking that they are mutually consistent evidence for the same conclusion.
Assuming electrolysis is always the 'advanced' or 'best' method and should therefore be recommended for any metal, regardless of why electrolysis is actually needed.

mcq.stem: Which statement correctly explains why aluminium is extracted by electrolysis rather than by carbon reduction?

options.text: Aluminium oxide does not contain oxygen atoms, so carbon reduction is not chemically possible
options.why_wrong: aluminium oxide, Al2O3, certainly contains oxygen; the issue is carbon's insufficient reactivity, not an absence of oxygen to remove.

options.text: Carbon reduction only works for non-metal elements, never for any metal oxide
options.why_wrong: carbon reduction is exactly the method used for iron, a metal; the limitation is about relative reactivity to carbon, not about metals versus non-metals.

options.text: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide
Electrolysis is simply the cheaper method for every metal, so it is chosen whenever available
options.why_wrong: electrolysis is generally more energy-intensive and expensive than carbon reduction; it is used for aluminium out of chemical necessity, not because it is cheaper.

mcq.explanation: Aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove oxygen from aluminium oxide at any practical temperature; electrolysis is used instead to force the reduction.

mcq.stem: What is the main ore of iron, and what is its formula?

options.text: Bauxite, Al2O3
options.why_wrong: bauxite is the ore associated with aluminium, not iron, and its formula shown here is also aluminium oxide, not an iron compound.

options.text: Limestone, CaCO3
options.why_wrong: limestone contains no iron at all; it is added to the furnace for a separate role, forming slag, not as the iron ore.

options.text: Coke, C
options.why_wrong: coke is nearly pure carbon, used as the reducing agent, not as the iron ore itself.

options.text: Hematite, Fe2O3

mcq.explanation: Hematite, iron(III) oxide (Fe2O3), is the main ore from which iron is extracted by reduction with carbon monoxide.

mcq.stem: What is the chemical role of limestone added to a blast furnace?

options.text: It decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silica impurities to form slag
It supplies additional iron to increase the yield
options.why_wrong: limestone (CaCO3) contains no iron atoms at all; it cannot supply any iron to the furnace.

options.text: It reacts directly with iron(III) oxide to reduce it to iron
options.why_wrong: iron(III) oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide, not by limestone or any of its decomposition products.

options.text: It cools the furnace to stop the iron from melting too quickly
options.why_wrong: the furnace is specifically designed to keep the iron molten; limestone's role is chemical (slag formation), not thermal cooling.

mcq.explanation: Limestone decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silica impurities in the ore to form molten calcium silicate (slag), removing impurities from the iron.

mcq.stem: A metal is found naturally only as small nuggets of the pure, uncombined element. What does this suggest about its extraction?

options.text: It must be extracted by electrolysis, since that is the most powerful method available
options.why_wrong: a metal found already uncombined needs no chemical reduction step at all; electrolysis would be solving a problem that does not exist for it.

options.text: It needs no chemical extraction step; only physical separation from the surrounding rock is required
It must be extracted by carbon reduction, since all metals require some chemical processing
options.why_wrong: a metal found as the pure element is not combined with oxygen in an ore, so there is no oxide present for carbon to reduce in the first place.

options.text: It cannot be identified as a metal until a chemical extraction method is found for it
options.why_wrong: being found as the pure, uncombined element is itself strong evidence the substance is a very unreactive metal; no extraction method is needed to establish this.

mcq.explanation: The least reactive metals, such as gold and silver, are often found native (uncombined), needing only physical separation from surrounding rock, not any chemical extraction step.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Carbon can reduce any metal oxide, including aluminium oxide, given a hot enough furnace.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Carbon reduction works for iron and is the only extraction method many learners meet first in detail, so it is generalised into a universal method for 'getting a metal out of its ore', with temperature treated as the only limiting factor.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner suggests heating aluminium oxide with carbon/coke in a furnace, the same way iron ore is treated, as a way to extract aluminium.
misconceptions.correct_model: Carbon can only reduce the oxides of metals below it in the reactivity series (such as iron); aluminium is more reactive than carbon, so carbon cannot remove the oxygen from aluminium oxide at any practical furnace temperature, which is exactly why aluminium requires electrolysis instead.
misconceptions.remediation: Ask the learner to locate both aluminium and carbon in the series, and apply the general rule (a less reactive element cannot remove oxygen bonded to a more reactive one) before considering temperature at all.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Limestone is the main source of the iron obtained from a blast furnace.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Limestone is a prominent, named input poured into the furnace alongside the iron ore, so without separating the inputs' roles, it can look like one of several 'iron sources' rather than a chemically distinct material.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes limestone as providing iron, or lists it as an alternative or additional iron ore.
misconceptions.correct_model: The iron comes entirely from the iron ore (hematite, $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$); limestone ($\mathrm{CaCO_{3}}$) contains no iron at all and plays a completely separate role, decomposing to calcium oxide, which then reacts with silica impurities in the ore to form molten slag, removing those impurities from the iron.
misconceptions.remediation: Write the chemical formula of each input (hematite Fe2O3, coke C, limestone CaCO3) side by side and ask which one(s) actually contain an iron atom.

misconceptions.incorrect_model: Slag is molten iron, or a form of impure iron.
misconceptions.why_it_appears: Slag and molten iron are both hot, dense, flowing liquids tapped from the same furnace, so without a clear chemical distinction they can look like two grades of the same substance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_signal: The learner describes slag as 'the dirty iron' or as iron contaminated with limestone.
misconceptions.correct_model: Slag is calcium silicate ($\mathrm{CaSiO_{3}}$), a compound formed from limestone's calcium oxide reacting with silica impurities from the ore; it contains no significant iron at all. Slag and molten iron are kept apart because slag, being less dense, floats above the denser molten iron and is tapped off separately, at a different, higher point in the furnace.
misconceptions.remediation: State the two materials' formulae side by side (Fe for molten iron; CaSiO3 for slag) and connect the density difference directly to why they separate into two distinct layers rather than mixing.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming carbon can reduce any metal oxide if the furnace is made hot enough.
common_mistakes.why: Carbon reduction is the first, most familiar extraction method met, so temperature looks like the only variable that could be limiting it.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Always compare the metal's position with carbon's position in the series first; if the metal is above carbon, no furnace temperature makes carbon reduction work.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing limestone as a source of iron, or as an alternative ore.
common_mistakes.why: Limestone is a prominent named input added alongside the actual iron ore, which can blur its very different chemical role.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Check the formula: CaCO3 contains no iron atoms at all; all the iron comes specifically from hematite, Fe2O3.

common_mistakes.mistake: Describing slag as impure or 'dirty' iron, rather than as a chemically distinct compound.
common_mistakes.why: Slag and molten iron are both hot, dense, flowing liquids tapped from the same furnace, so they can look like two grades of one material.
common_mistakes.how_to_avoid: Name slag by its formula, CaSiO3, and state explicitly that it contains no significant iron, floating above the molten iron purely because it is less dense.

exam_notes: When explaining an extraction method, always compare the metal's position specifically with carbon's, not with any other single metal, since the carbon boundary is what actually decides electrolysis versus carbon reduction.
Give a balanced equation for every named furnace reaction asked for; a correctly named reaction without its balanced equation will usually not gain full credit.
State explicitly which product (iron or slag) each furnace reaction leads to, rather than listing equations without connecting them to the two separate outputs.

summary.big_idea: A metal's position in the reactivity series, specifically relative to carbon, determines whether it must be extracted by electrolysis, by reduction with carbon, or needs no chemical extraction at all because it is found native.
key_points: Metals more reactive than carbon (potassium to aluminium) are extracted by electrolysis; carbon cannot reduce their oxides at any practical temperature.
Metals below carbon (zinc, iron, copper) are extracted by reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide; the least reactive metals (silver, gold) are often found native.
Iron is extracted from hematite (Fe2O3) in a blast furnace: coke and hot air generate carbon monoxide, which reduces Fe2O3 to molten iron.
Limestone contains no iron; it decomposes to calcium oxide, which reacts with silica impurities to form slag (CaSiO3), separating impurities from the iron.
summary.what_to_remember_if_nothing_else: Compare the metal's position with carbon's: above carbon needs electrolysis, below carbon can use carbon reduction, and the least reactive metals are often found native.

exit_check.question: A newly discovered metal is found to react with dilute acid more vigorously than iron but less vigorously than zinc. Predict which extraction method it would need, and justify your answer.
exit_check.answer: This places the metal between zinc and iron in the series, which is below carbon's position; it could therefore be extracted by reduction with carbon (or carbon monoxide), since carbon is more reactive than the metal and can remove the oxygen from its oxide. Electrolysis is not needed.

exercises.statement: The data below was obtained by carrying out displacement reactions of five metals (A-E) with the nitrates of the same five metals. Strips of each metal were placed in solutions of the other four metals' nitrate solutions. The results are given in a 5x5 table (rows = metal strip used, columns = nitrate solution tested): Metal A displaced the metal from nitrates B, C and D, but not from nitrate E. Metal B did not displace the metal from any of the other nitrates (A, C, D or E). Metal C displaced the metal from nitrates B and D, but not from A or E. Metal D displaced the metal from nitrate B only (not from A, C or E). Metal E displaced the metal from all four other nitrates (A, B, C and D). (✓ = metal displaced, ✗ = no reaction). Put the five metals A-E in order of their reactivity, using the data above.
exercises.answer: Order of reactivity (most to least reactive): E > A > C > D > B.
exercises.full_solution:
In a displacement reaction the metal that is placed in solution (the strip) only displaces the metal ion from the nitrate solution if it is MORE reactive than the metal already in that solution. So a ✓ in row X, column Y means metal X is more reactive than metal Y, and a ✗ means X is less reactive than Y (or they are too similar to react).

Reading off the table: A beats B, C and D, but loses to E, so A is below only E. B beats nobody, so B is the least reactive of the five. C beats B and D, but loses to A and E, so C sits between A and D. D only beats B, so D is more reactive than B but less reactive than A, C and E. E beats all four others, so E is the most reactive.

Putting these pairwise results together consistently (Checking every one of the 20 cells in the table against the ordering and none contradicted it) gives a single unambiguous reactivity order from most to least reactive: E, A, C, D, B.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Write equations for the reaction between: (a) aluminium and moderately concentrated hydrochloric acid; (b) aluminium and moderately concentrated sodium hydroxide (producing sodium aluminate, NaAl(OH)4).
exercises.answer:
(a) $2Al(s) + 6HCl(aq) \rightarrow 2AlCl_3(aq) + 3H_2(g)$
(b) $2Al(s) + 2NaOH(aq) + 6H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaAl(OH)_4(aq) + 3H_2(g)$
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Aluminium reacts with hydrochloric acid like any reactive metal with a dilute/moderately concentrated acid: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen. Aluminium is a group with a +3 ion, so the salt is aluminium chloride, AlCl3. Balancing: 2 Al atoms are needed to match the 3 Cl per AlCl3 unit (2 AlCl3 needs 6 Cl, i.e. 6 HCl), and the 6 H from the 6 HCl become 3 H2 molecules. This gives 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl3 + 3H2, which balances: Al 2=2, H 6=6, Cl 6=6 – balanced.

(b) Aluminium is amphoteric, so unlike most metals it also reacts with a strong alkali, not just acids. With moderately concentrated sodium hydroxide solution the products are hydrogen gas and sodium aluminate, given here as NaAl(OH)4. Since this product already contains 4 oxygens/hydrogens from (OH) groups, water must also appear on the reactant side to supply the extra oxygen and hydrogen (the reaction only works in the presence of water). Balancing by inspection: 2Al + 2NaOH + 6H2O → 2NaAl(OH)4 + 3H2 (Al 2=2, Na 2=2, O 8=8, H 14=14 – balanced).
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: How does the method used for extracting a metal from its ore depend on the metal's position in the reactivity series?
exercises.answer: The more reactive a metal, the harder (more energy-intensive) the extraction method needed: very reactive metals (e.g. sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium) must be extracted by electrolysis of a molten compound; moderately reactive metals (e.g. zinc, iron) can be extracted by reduction with carbon or carbon monoxide (or, for zinc, sometimes by electrolysis); unreactive metals (e.g. silver, gold) are often found native (uncombined) or need only mild treatment to obtain the pure metal.
exercises.full_solution:
A metal's position in the reactivity series tells you how strongly its atoms 'want' to hold on to the electrons they lost when they formed compounds in the ore – the more reactive the metal, the more stable (harder to reduce) its compound is, so more energy/stronger reducing conditions are needed to get the metal back out.

- Most reactive metals (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al): their oxides/compounds are too stable to be reduced by carbon, so they are extracted by electrolysis of the molten ore/compound (e.g. molten aluminium oxide dissolved in cryolite for aluminium). This needs a lot of electrical energy.
- Moderately reactive metals (Zn, Fe, Pb, Cu): these oxides can be reduced by heating with carbon (coke) or carbon monoxide, which is cheaper than electrolysis – for example iron is extracted in a blast furnace by reduction with carbon monoxide.
- Unreactive metals (Ag, Au, and to an extent Cu): these are so unreactive that they are sometimes found uncombined (native) in the Earth's crust, or their compounds are so unstable that only simple heating, or displacement by a more reactive metal, is needed to release the pure metal.

So as you go up the reactivity series, the extraction method generally moves from 'found native/simple reduction' → 'reduction with carbon/carbon monoxide' → 'electrolysis', i.e. it becomes more difficult and energy-demanding.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: 'It is true to say that almost all the reactions by which a metal is extracted from its ore are reduction reactions.' Discuss this statement with respect to the extraction of iron, aluminium and zinc.
exercises.answer: The statement is true: in every case the metal ion (positively charged, as found in the ore) gains electrons to become the neutral metal atom, which is by definition a reduction, whether that electron transfer is driven by a chemical reducing agent (carbon/carbon monoxide) or by an electric current.
exercises.full_solution:
Reduction means gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen). In an ore, the metal is present as a positive ion (e.g. Fe3+ in Fe2O3, Al3+ in Al2O3, Zn2+ in ZnO); extracting the metal always means converting that ion back into neutral metal atoms, which requires the ion to gain electrons – so by definition every extraction is a reduction, no matter which method is used.

- Iron: in the blast furnace, haematite (Fe2O3) is reduced by carbon monoxide: Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2 (checked: Fe 2=2, O 6=6, C 3=3 – balanced). Here CO is the reducing agent: it gains oxygen (becoming CO2), while the iron(III) oxide loses oxygen and the Fe3+ ions gain electrons.
- Aluminium: aluminium oxide is far too stable to be reduced by carbon, so it is reduced electrolytically instead. Molten Al2O3 (dissolved in cryolite) is electrolysed: at the cathode, Al3+ + 3e− → Al. The gain of electrons at the cathode is a reduction, even though no carbon is involved: 2Al2O3 → 4Al + 3O2 overall (checked: Al 4=4, O 6=6 – balanced).
- Zinc: zinc oxide can be reduced by heating with carbon, ZnO + C → Zn + CO (checked: Zn 1=1, O 1=1, C 1=1 – balanced), or zinc can instead be extracted electrolytically after converting the ore to a zinc sulfate solution, again reducing Zn2+ to Zn at the cathode.

So whether the reducing agent is carbon/carbon monoxide (iron, zinc) or an electric current supplying electrons directly (aluminium, and sometimes zinc), the key chemical step is always a reduction of the metal ion to the metal. The statement is therefore correct.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Titanium is extracted from rutile (TiO2). Use your research skills, including the Internet, to suggest the detail of the extraction process.
exercises.answer: Titanium is extracted by the Kroll process: rutile (TiO2) is first converted to titanium(IV) chloride by heating with chlorine gas and carbon, and the TiCl4 is then reduced to titanium metal using molten magnesium (or sodium) under an inert argon atmosphere.
exercises.full_solution:
Titanium cannot be extracted simply by reduction with carbon (it would form very stable titanium carbide instead), so a two-stage process called the Kroll process is used.

Stage 1 – chlorination: purified rutile ore is heated with chlorine gas and coke (carbon) to convert the oxide into a chloride, which is easier to reduce and purify by distillation: TiO2 + 2Cl2 + 2C → TiCl4 + 2CO (checked: Ti 1=1, O 2=2, Cl 4=4, C 2=2 – balanced). The TiCl4 produced is a liquid at room temperature and can be purified by fractional distillation.

Stage 2 – reduction: the purified TiCl4 vapour is then reduced using molten magnesium metal, in a sealed reactor filled with argon gas (so that no oxygen or nitrogen can react with the very reactive hot titanium or magnesium): TiCl4 + 2Mg → Ti + 2MgCl2 (checked: Ti 1=1, Cl 4=4, Mg 2=2 – balanced). The magnesium chloride by-product is removed, and the magnesium can be recovered and recycled by electrolysis.

An inert atmosphere and the extra chlorination step are needed because titanium is reactive enough to react with oxygen, nitrogen and carbon at the high temperatures involved, which is also why the whole process is expensive and titanium metal costs much more than iron or aluminium.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Many local authorities collect used cans from households. The cans collected can be made from different metals such as aluminium and iron. How could cans made of iron be separated easily from aluminium cans?
exercises.answer: By magnetic separation: iron (steel) cans are magnetic and are pulled out by a strong magnet (e.g. an overhead magnet on a conveyor belt), while aluminium cans are not magnetic and are left behind.
exercises.full_solution: Iron and steel are magnetic materials, whereas aluminium is not magnetic at all. In a recycling plant, the mixed cans are passed along a conveyor belt under (or past) a powerful magnet. The magnet attracts and lifts out every iron/steel can, leaving the non-magnetic aluminium cans on the belt to be collected separately. This is quick, cheap and does not require sorting by hand, which is why magnetic separation is the standard method used to split steel cans from aluminium cans at recycling centres.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: As well as saving money in terms of energy costs, what other reasons could be given to promote recycling of aluminium cans?
exercises.answer: Recycling conserves limited bauxite ore reserves, reduces the environmental damage caused by mining/quarrying (habitat destruction, scarred landscapes, noise and dust), cuts down on landfill waste, and lowers greenhouse-gas and other pollutant emissions associated with extracting and processing new aluminium.
exercises.full_solution: Beyond the direct saving in electricity (recycling uses only about 5% of the energy of extracting new aluminium by electrolysis), there are several other benefits: it conserves the finite supply of bauxite ore so that it lasts longer for future generations; it avoids the environmental damage of quarrying/mining new bauxite, such as destruction of habitats, scarring of the landscape, and the dust/noise produced; it reduces the amount of waste sent to landfill sites, which are themselves limited in space and can cause local pollution; and because less electricity generation is needed (much of which still comes from burning fossil fuels), recycling indirectly reduces carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gas emissions, helping to limit the contribution to climate change.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Calcium oxide is a base. It combines with solid, acidic oxides in the basic oxygen furnace. Write a chemical equation for one of these oxides reacting with the added lime.
exercises.answer: $CaO(s) + SiO_2(s) \rightarrow CaSiO_3(l)$ (calcium silicate slag).
exercises.full_solution:
In steelmaking (the basic oxygen furnace), impure molten iron from the blast furnace still contains acidic non-metal oxide impurities such as silicon dioxide (from sand/silica in the ore) and phosphorus oxides. Calcium oxide (quicklime) is added as a base to neutralise these acidic oxides, forming a molten calcium salt called 'slag' which floats on top of the liquid steel and can be poured off.

Taking silicon dioxide as the example acidic oxide: CaO (base) + SiO2 (acidic oxide) → CaSiO3 (calcium silicate, the slag). This is a simple acid-base combination reaction. Checking atoms: 1 Ca = 1 Ca, 1 Si = 1 Si, and oxygen: left-hand side has 1 (from CaO) + 2 (from SiO2) = 3, right-hand side CaSiO3 has 3 oxygens – balanced with no further coefficients needed.

(An equally valid alternative, if phosphorus(V) oxide is chosen instead, is 6CaO + P4O10 → 2Ca3(PO4)2, forming calcium phosphate slag.)
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: 'Many metals are more useful to us when mixed with some other elements.' Discuss this statement with respect to stainless steel.
exercises.answer: True: pure iron on its own is relatively soft and rusts easily, but alloying it with carbon (to make ordinary steel) makes it much harder, and further alloying with chromium and nickel (to make stainless steel) also makes it resistant to corrosion, producing a metal that is far more useful for cutlery, kitchen equipment, surgical instruments and exhaust systems than pure iron would be.
exercises.full_solution:
Pure iron is a soft metal that corrodes (rusts) quickly in the presence of air and water, which limits how useful it is on its own. Mixing (alloying) it with other elements changes its properties for the better.

First, adding a small amount of the non-metal carbon to iron produces ordinary steel, which is much harder and stronger than pure iron because the carbon atoms distort the regular layers of iron atoms, making it harder for those layers to slide over each other.

Second, adding the metals chromium and nickel to steel produces stainless steel. The chromium reacts with oxygen in the air to form a thin, tough, continuous layer of chromium oxide on the surface, which protects the iron underneath from rusting (unlike the flaky iron oxide that forms on untreated steel). The nickel adds further hardness and toughness to the alloy.

The result is a material – stainless steel – that is harder than pure iron and resistant to corrosion, which is why it is chosen for cutlery, kitchen sinks, surgical instruments and car exhaust systems, uses for which pure iron would be unsuitable (too soft and it would rust). This supports the statement: mixing iron with carbon, chromium and nickel makes it considerably more useful than the pure metal alone.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)

exercises.statement: Name the metals used in the production of these alloys: (a) brass; (b) zinc amalgam; (c) bronze; (d) solder.
exercises.answer: (a) Brass: copper and zinc. (b) Zinc amalgam: zinc and mercury. (c) Bronze: copper and tin. (d) Solder: tin and lead.
exercises.full_solution:
(a) Brass is an alloy of copper and zinc; it has a gold-like appearance and is harder and more corrosion-resistant than either pure metal, which is why it is used for door knobs, musical instruments and plumbing fittings.
(b) An amalgam is, by definition, any alloy that contains mercury; zinc amalgam is therefore an alloy of zinc and mercury.
(c) Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin; it is harder than copper alone and has traditionally been used for statues, bells and some tools/coins.
(d) Solder (traditional tin-lead solder, as commonly used before lead-free alternatives became standard) is an alloy of tin and lead, chosen because it has a lower melting point than either metal alone, making it useful for joining electrical components and metal pipework.
exercises.source_book: Cambridge IGCSE Combined and Co-ordinated Sciences (Hodder/Cambridge, dokumen.pub edition)
